title: Leveraging AI for More Effective Teams: Evidence-Based Strategies for Diverse Idea Generation

detail.title: Leveraging AI for More Effective Teams: Evidence-Based Strategies for Diverse Idea Generation
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy generative artificial intelligence to augment team brainstorming and idea generation processes. While AI-powered tools such as large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable capacity to produce high-quality ideas at scale, recent research reveals a critical limitation: AI-generated idea pools exhibit lower diversity than those produced by human groups, potentially constraining innovation outcomes. This article synthesizes emerging evidence on AI's role in team ideation, examining how prompt engineering techniques-particularly Chain-of-Thought prompting-can substantially increase idea variance and cognitive diversity. Drawing on experimental findings and organizational cases across technology, consumer goods, and professional services sectors, we identify evidence-based practices for hybrid human-AI ideation systems. Organizations that strategically combine multiple prompting approaches, preserve human judgment in selection and synthesis, and structure AI interactions to maximize exploration rather than exploitation can achieve idea pools rivaling or exceeding purely human teams in both volume and diversity. The implications extend beyond product innovation to strategic planning, problem-solving, and creative work across industries.

title: From Liminality to Communitas: The Collective Dimensions of Transformative Learning
affiliations: Adler University, Michigan State University, Wayne State University, DDJ Myers LTD and Rutgers University

detail.title: From Liminality to Communitas: The Collective Dimensions of Transformative Learning
detail.abstract: This article addresses a significant gap in the transformative learning literature as it relates to collective transformation, a transformation that is a level beyond individual transformation and is differentiated from the designed and imposed forms of social or organizational change. We consider collective transformation as an emergent and shared worldview shift that is grounded in a shared experience. The participants might not be fully aware of or even able to describe this experience until they engage with it at the interpersonal level. In prior research and practice, the five authors have independently observed and documented the phenomenon of collective transformation among members of marginalized populations who have undergone liminal experiences--forms of disequilibrium that leave individuals betwixt and between. The common thread in these experiences is the emergence of a shared feeling called "communitas," which is a deeply felt (yet often temporary) sense of belonging and community. This study's purpose is to further explore the roles that states of liminality and "communitas" play in creating the conditions for collective transformation. We draw on several theoretical and practice-based areas of literature and on five particular types of experience. We then examine each case for shared experiences of liminality and "communitas" as well as for the underlying qualities of self-understanding, relational ability, and a collectively felt sense of new possibilities. This study also includes suggestions for the application of these concepts to other social groups and in other contexts.

title: The Genius Allocation Problem: How Transformative AI Reshapes Knowledge Work and Organizational Design

detail.title: The Genius Allocation Problem: How Transformative AI Reshapes Knowledge Work and Organizational Design
detail.abstract: The emergence of transformative artificial intelligence systems capable of genius-level cognitive work fundamentally challenges traditional organizational models for allocating knowledge workers. This article examines how organizations should strategically deploy human experts, routine knowledge workers, and AI systems across different types of problems based on distance from established knowledge. Drawing on recent economic theory, we demonstrate that optimal allocation depends on recognizing distinct comparative advantages: AI excels at moderately novel problems, human experts at frontier challenges furthest from existing knowledge, and routine workers at applying established frameworks. In the short term, AI introduction pushes human experts toward ultra-specialized frontier work. Long-term, organizations may witness complete displacement of routine knowledge work unless AI efficiency parameters favor human application of existing knowledge. Organizations that master this three-tier allocation problem will capture disproportionate value from the AI transition while preserving meaningful roles for human expertise at the knowledge frontier.

detail.abstract: Technological evolution is often conceptualized as incremental or disruptive, yet the mechanisms driving systemic innovation remain underexplored. This paper introduces the concept of technological macroevolution, arguing that the evolution of complex technologies depends on the progressive enhancement of embedded subsystems. Drawing on evolutionary theory, we extend existing models of technological change by framing subsystem microevolution as a primary driver of systemic innovation. Using a longitudinal case study of the iPhone (2007-2025) and its interaction with Bluetooth and other subsystems, we show that successive Bluetooth versions (2.0-6.0) consistently preceded major iPhone advancements, reducing integration lags from three to one year and accelerating co-evolution. Exponential improvements in camera resolution and display quality further shaped the macroevolutionary trajectory of smartphones. Hedonic pricing analysis identifies battery life and display resolution as key determinants of innovation and market value. Theoretical contribution lies in reconceptualizing technological change as a hierarchical evolutionary process, where subsystem dynamics govern systemic progress. Policy and managerial implications suggest that innovation strategies should prioritize monitoring and investing in critical subsystems to anticipate system-level breakthroughs. This perspective informs technology forecasting, R&D allocation, and competitive positioning in environments characterized by rapid technological interdependence.

detail.abstract:
Set in June 2025, this case follows Christie Carpenter, managing director of private investments at DRC Partners (DRC), as she evaluates a proposed continuation vehicle (CV) for ClerkMD Inc. (ClerkMD), a high-performing health information management company in Evermore Capital Partners' (Evermore's) Fund III portfolio. After a $265 million sale prospect unexpectedly collapsed, DRC and Evermore explored using a CV to extend ownership, provide additional capital for ClerkMD's next growth phase, and offer existing limited partners—including DRC—the option to take liquidity or reinvest. Although CVs had become increasingly common in private equity, neither DRC nor Evermore had previously executed one, and Carpenter remained concerned about conflicts of interest, valuation challenges, and the need for alignment among multiple stakeholder groups. Were Carpenter and DRC ready to sail ClerkMD's ship into the next frontier of private equity financial innovation?This case pairs well with the technical note "An Introduction to Private Equity Secondaries" (UVA-F-2123), which outlines the mechanics of transactions led by both limited parters and general partners, the creation and operation of CVs, and the sources of conflict and information asymmetry that are central to Carpenter's decision.

Excerpt

Have Your ClerkMD and Sell It Too

On a balmy Monday morning in June 2025, Christie Carpenter, managing director of private investments at DRC Partners (DRC), was collecting her thoughts about a potential investment in a continuation vehicle (CV) transaction. DRC—a multifamily office with $8.6 billion in assets under management (AUM)—allocated about 34% of its portfolio to alternative assets. It was a respected limited partner (LP) for a number of middle-market private equity (PE) funds and was capable of committing between $25 million and $50 million of capital. Yet CVs represented a new frontier for both DRC and Carpenter.

The proposed CV transaction involved ClerkMD Inc. (ClerkMD), a player in the health information management (HIM) industry. ClerkMD was a portfolio company of Evermore Health Fund III, to which DRC had committed $30 million in 2017. DRC had invested in the last five of Evermore Capital Partners' (Evermore's) funds, including two health care–focused ones, housed under the Evermore Health name. Carpenter's team believed in Evermore's investment philosophy, and in an experienced management team led by Ben Forde, Evermore Health's vertical managing partner and a health care industry veteran.

Evermore's journey with ClerkMD started in 2018, when Evermore Health Fund III invested $15.5 million in return for a 52.1% stake in the company. Since then, the Evermore team had invested a lot of effort in pushing ClerkMD to a new stage of growth and development. Under the team's watchful eye, ClerkMD had flourished. The company's revenue increased 7.5×, from $8 million in 2018 to almost $60 million in 2024, and it was expected to continue growing at double-digit rates. ClerkMD secured prominent clients, underscoring its product quality and credibility, and it steadily gained market share at the expense of much larger competitors. ClerkMD also diversified its offerings by introducing new lines of business that boasted higher margins. In addition, the company had tremendous future potential in the form of add-on acquisitions that could expand both the product offerings that were under one roof and the client base.

title: Europe, 1945 to 1952: First Steps to Unification?
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business and University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Europe, 1945 to 1952: First Steps to Unification?

publicationDetails.journalName: Darden Case Collection

detail.abstract:
After World War II, Europe was in ruins. From these circumstances a vision of a unified Europe was born, and thus the initial steps of the European Union (EU) took place from 1945 to 1952. This technical note discusses the events of the years leading to the EU's beginnings, including the reasons for unification and the early economic cooperation. The note also introduces students to the concept of fiscal federalism and provides a framework to consider how resources and tasks can be allocated to different levels of government.

Excerpt

Europe, 1945 to 1952: First Steps to Unification?

On May 8, 1945, World War II in Europe—the western peninsula of Eurasia—came to an end with Germany's unconditional surrender. In Europe, between 15 million and 20 million people had been killed, according to one estimate. Industrial European countries were largely left bereft of resources. “Europe was in ruins and reduced to total confusion: factories and transport links destroyed, traditional trade dislocated, livestock wiped out and shortages in raw materials and foodstuffs prevalent,” wrote the Centre virtuel de la connaissance sur l'Europe (CVCE). As expected, the GDP of most European countries was set back decades. For example, the Austrian GDP in 1945 was equivalent to its GDP in 1886, France's was equivalent to 1891, and Italy's was equivalent to 1909. The war had started on September 1, 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, and, because of their defense treaty obligations with Poland, France and Great Britian declared war on Germany.

War between European countries was not new. One only needed to remember the Seven Years War, the Napoleonic Wars, the Franco-Prussian (also known as the Franco-German) War, and World War I. That said, “The Second World War was the most destructive conflict in human history,” wrote the Imperial War Museum. “The decisions that led to war reflected the ambitions, rivalries, fears and anxieties that developed in the two decades that followed the end of the First World War. The European powers were willing to go to war to extend or protect what each nation saw—in dramatically different ways—as matters of vital interest, great power status, international prestige, and national survival.” World War II, it should be noted, was the third war since 1870 in which France and Germany had fought each other. The first—the Franco-Prussian War—ended with France's defeat and nearly three years of German occupation. France's influence and power declined while Germany became a “technologically and industrially superior nation that by the first decade of the 20th century had built the most powerful land army on the European continent.” World War II saw Germany invade France with the French surrendering 17 days later on June 22, 1940. These wars had taken their toll on the minds of the French people. After World War II, only 10% to 20% of French people believed they could trust the Germans.

European scholars Richard Baldwin and Charles Wyplosz named three causes of World War II that were debated by Europeans following the war: Germany's reactions to France and Britain taking German land and imposing reparations on Germany because of its role in World War I; Marxist/Leninist reactions to the spread of capitalism; and nationalism. They opined that however European leaders and countries reacted in the wake of the war's destruction, it would be informed by how they framed the causes.

Entering 2025, the European Union (EU) finds itself at a pivotal moment, caught between internal demands for social cohesion and external forces of global competition, climate change, and geopolitical realignments. The EU relies on myriad institutions, bodies, and decentralized agencies to function. At the forefront are five key institutions, or “the Big 5”: the European Commission, the Council of the European Union, the European Parliament, the Court of Justice of the European Union, and the European Council. This technical note provides an overview of these institutions and the EU's legislative process. It examines the EU's decision-making process (i.e., its efficiency), discusses fiscal federalism (i.e., task allocation at the governmental levels), and considers the EU's democratic legitimacy in the context of principal-agent theory. The single market and the EU's competitiveness are also discussed. The technical note ultimately asks students to consider what reforms may be necessary for the EU to reach its full potential.

title: The EU's Banking Union: Is it Doomed?

detail.title: The EU's Banking Union: Is it Doomed?

publicationDetails.journalName: Darden Case Collection

detail.abstract:
Since 2014, the European Union (EU) had been trying to establish a single banking union based on three pillars—supervision, resolution, and depositor insurance. While EU member states had quickly agreed to a set of mechanisms on bank supervision and resolution, years later, they continued to disagree on depositor insurance. Part of the objective of the banking union was to break the doom loop—the connection between banks and their own governments. This case provides a brief overview of banking in the EU and goes into detail on the supervision and resolution mechanisms, including roles at the EU level versus at the sovereign level. It also delves into different viewpoints and several proposals on establishing depositor insurance for students to consider, including concerns of moral hazard and the possible role of safe assets.The case is taught in “EU in the World Economy,” a second-year elective course at the University of Virginia Darden School of Business. To prepare business students for global business experience, this course explores the fundamental differences and similarities between the EU and the United States. The case is also useful for a general economics course discussing moral hazard, adverse selection, and deposit insurance or, alternatively, in a course focusing on the economics of banking.

Excerpt

The EU's Banking Union: Is It Doomed?

In early 2024, the European Commission (Commission) put forth a proposal to amend a 2014 regulation, (EU) 806/2014, in order to establish a European Deposit Insurance Scheme (EDIS), the final and third pillar of the European Union (EU) banking union. The work toward completing another of the four freedoms of the EU to complete the banking union began in 2014 when the European Central Bank (ECB) assumed prudential supervisory authority over euro-area banks from their respective member-state bodies. With the formation of a European banking union, leaders hoped to establish a more standardized approach to banking and break the connections between banks and their home governments—known as the “doom loop”—that had contributed to prior economic hardships. Yet 10 years later, the banking union remained incomplete and in doubt.

Three pillars were at the heart of an EU banking union and the transfer of sovereignty over the supervision and regulation of national banking systems from the member states to a central body: (1) supervision, (2) resolution, and (3) depositor insurance. Pillars 1 and 2 had been agreed on and implemented quickly, but in 2024, Pillar 3, the final piece needed to complete an EU banking union, remained missing. Historically, member states in the south wanted a pan-EU deposit insurance system, while northern member states would not accept one without stricter regulations on bank holdings of their own government's debt. “An agreement on a common deposit insurance was hampered by the weak state of the banks in some peripheral countries, with Germany fearing that it would have to pay for Italian banks,” said one senior fellow at the Centre for European Policy Studies. A Bruegel senior fellow said in 2023,

In a way, governments are of two minds. On the one hand, they understand that completing the banking union is necessary for the eurozone to be resilient, and they want the eurozone to be resilient sincerely. But at the same time, there are so many aspects of the linkages they have with national banking sectors that they like and don't want to get rid of…This kind of thing only makes progress when there's a big crisis. And sorry if what I say sounds too cynical, but I think at this point there isn't a big banking crisis in the eurozone.

detail.title: Ex-ante Novelty Predicts Ex-post Quality of AI Innovation among World's Top R&D Investors
detail.abstract: We use patent filing data to compute two ex-ante technological novelty indices. We crossreference patent data with firm-level data of top R&D investors to study the predictive power of the patent-level novelty indices for ex-post patent quality. We focus on patents relevant to Artificial Intelligence (AI), a fast-developing field still emerging, and estimate for the patenting outcome and for whether the patent is in the top 1% cited high-impact group. We find strong evidence that the ex-ante technological novelty measures correlate robustly with the ex-post quality of an invention. Our work also offers an updated methodology for identifying AI-patents.

Excerpt

Mastercard Academy 2.0: Striving for More

More than a year had passed since Nur Hasan, social impact manager at the Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth (CFIG), had placed his ballot in the 2024 Indonesian general election. Now in April 2025, Hasan's daily work was running smoothly as the new administration, led by President Prabowo Subianto, continued CFIG's partnerships with government ministries. In the last four years of President Joko Widodo's term, Hasan and CFIG had successfully launched and completed Mastercard Academy 2.0 (MA 2.0), a first-of-its-kind program that taught digital skills to nearly 200,000 Indonesian schoolgirls, secondary school students, entrepreneurs, and mid-career professionals. Several government partnerships were critical to support and scale the program past its initial goals.

The largest subprogram of MA 2.0, a digital mentorship and training platform for entrepreneurs and professionals, was now expanding into an independent follow-up program, Mastercard Strive in Indonesia (Strive Indonesia). Launched in April 2023, Strive Indonesia set a goal of supporting 300,000 micro and small enterprises (MSEs) by April 2026. As of April 2025, the program had reached 102,000 MSEs, 65% of which were women-led or -owned. Some of the digital strategies that worked so well under MA 2.0 were not as successful for Strive Indonesia. Still, Hasan felt hopeful about reaching the target. He said, “This year should be easier compared to the first two years because the partnership with the government, including with 10 regencies, is secure, and the partnerships with some private-sector firms including 15 financial services providers [FSPs] were already secured last year.” With the end of the program in sight, how could Hasan make the most of Strive Indonesia's resources to reach more MSEs?

title: Beyond Amplification: The Resonance Cascade of Diplomatic Influence (RCDI): A Conceptual Framework for Small-State Diplomacy in a Polycentric World

detail.title: Beyond Amplification: The Resonance Cascade of Diplomatic Influence (RCDI): A Conceptual Framework for Small-State Diplomacy in a Polycentric World
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Resonance Cascade of Diplomatic Influence (RCDI) as an original conceptual framework for understanding how small states can generate disproportionate impact within an increasingly polycentric international system. Building upon the earlier Diplomacy of Proportional Amplification (DoPA), RCDI theorizes that diplomatic influence does not depend primarily on material power but on the strategic precision, coherence, and timing of a state’s communicative actions. Through the lens of resonance—rather than amplification—this framework explains how calibrated diplomatic “signals” can trigger cascading effects across multilateral, scientific, and narrative networks. Drawing on small-state praxis, particularly within the context of Small Island Developing States (SIDS), RCDI synthesizes insights from soft-power theory, constructivism, and complexity science to reveal how legitimacy and relational intelligence replace coercion as engines of global influence. The paper situates RCDI within contemporary debates in Global International Relations, proposes operational modalities for policy design, and identifies pathways for empirical testing through network and discourse analysis. By recentering small-state diplomacy as a generator of systemic resonance, RCDI contributes a new theoretical vocabulary for equitable influence in global governance.

In order to enable the application of the ijtihad method in the humanities, this article explores the leadership style in Islamic management, using Islamic teachings and based on ijtihad analysis.

Findings of this study show that ijtihad method is a combined method that is related to the combined knowledge of management from the branches of humanities and the method of Islamic leadership as one of the subjects of humanities in the field of ijtihad method can be analyzed. Considering the ijtihad method in Islamic teachings, there are two categories of propositions, in both of which there is a part of Quranic propositions and a part of narrative propositions.

Some of the first category statements directly depict the ruler or leader's relationship with followers and how they interact with them; However, some of these statements are general speeches that can be applied to the style of absolute softness; Therefore, it can be said that this category of propositions implies softness and absolute friendliness, and the second category of Qur'anic and narrative propositions emphasizes the mixing of softness with intensity of action; According to these two categories of propositions, according to the principles of jurisprudence and jurisprudence in the ijtihad method, it is possible to be in the position of a combination of propositions wherever a group of propositions (arguments) imply an absolute subject, at the same time a group Other propositions imply the same subject, carried absolute propositions to the constraint; What is more, according to the rule of "the plural is important, the first possibility of my plan", the arguments that are absolute can be carried on, so it can be inferred that in the leadership style, both flexibility and intensity of action are necessary; Hence, the result of ijtihad analysis is that leadership in Islamic management is a mixture of "maximum flexibility and minimum intensity."

title: Features of Digital Currency Circulation in the Russian Federation: Legal and Economic Analysis

detail.title: Features of Digital Currency Circulation in the Russian Federation: Legal and Economic Analysis
detail.abstract: This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the legal regime governing the circulation of digital currencies (cryptocurrencies) in the Russian Federation, a jurisdiction characterized by a uniquely contradictory and evolving regulatory approach. The research examines the existing legislative framework, primarily Federal Law No. 259-FZ "On Digital Financial Assets" (DFA), and its critical limitations, which effectively exclude cryptocurrency from the legal definition of a permitted means of payment, while allowing for its recognition as property. The methodological basis combines comparative legal analysis, economic analysis of law, and examination of law enforcement practice. The paper systematically explores key "features" (особенности) of the Russian model: the formal ban on using digital currency as a means of payment for goods and services; the legal uncertainty surrounding transactions like exchange, purchase/sale, and inheritance; the emerging regulatory sandbox for international settlements in digital assets; and the stark contrast between the prohibitive stance of the Bank of Russia and the more pragmatic proposals of the Ministry of Finance. The main conclusions indicate that the current model creates significant risks for participants (lack of judicial protection for transactions) while failing to curb the actual existence of a gray market. The study argues that Russia is moving toward a dual-track system: a complete domestic ban to ensure financial sovereignty, coupled with experimental use in foreign trade to circumvent sanctions. The work contributes to the global discourse on cryptocurrency regulation by detailing a unique case of "controlled prohibition.

detail.title: State Regulation of Cryptocurrency Mining in the Russian Federation
detail.abstract: This study examines the evolving legal framework for cryptocurrency mining in the Russian Federation, an activity that exists in a regulatory gray area between formal prohibition and de facto tolerance. The research analyzes the current legislative landscape, including the draft federal law "On Mining," the law on Digital Financial Assets (DFA), and the contrasting positions of key government institutions, primarily the Central Bank of the Russian Federation and the Ministry of Finance. The methodological approach is based on a comparative legal analysis of existing and proposed regulations, combined with an assessment of their economic and technological feasibility. The paper identifies the core contradictions in the state's approach: the desire to control a energy-intensive industry and capitalize on its export potential versus concerns over financial sovereignty, money laundering risks, and environmental impact. The main findings highlight the lack of a unified legal definition for mining, the unresolved issues of energy tariffs and connection to grids for miners, and the uncertainty regarding the legalization of cryptocurrency as a means of payment or an asset. The study concludes that the future model of regulation will likely be restrictive and focused on licensed industrial mining within experimental legal regimes, with a complete ban on private and "gray" mining. The contribution of this work lies in a systematic presentation of the current regulatory dilemma in Russia, which is relevant for both policymakers and participants of the digital asset market.

Appreciation is also conveyed to informants who participated in this study for their valuable contributions

detail.abstract: This study aims to develop a comprehensive overtourism measurement matrix for Bali by integrating Doxey's Irritation Index (Irridex) with the local Tri Hita Karana philosophy, thereby providing an analytical and practical tool for sustainable tourism governance. The research responds to intensifying overtourism pressures in Canggu, Ubud, Sanur, Tanah Lot, and Lovina, which increasingly threaten ecological balance, socioeconomic stability, and spiritual-cultural integrity. Employing a sequential explanatory mixed-methods approach, the study combined quantitative surveys with qualitative interviews involving 30 informants representing academia, community, industry, and government stakeholders. The proposed matrix assesses overtourism impacts across the three Tri Hita Karana dimensions Palemahan (ecological), Pawongan (social-economic), and Parahyangan (spiritual-cultural) while mapping residents' perceptions along Doxey's attitudinal stages: euphoria, apathy, annoyance, and antagonism. Findings reveal severe pressure and growing social fragmentation in southern tourism zones, with evidence of antagonistic attitudes and erosion of community harmony, while Lovina and Tanah Lot display emerging risks. North and East Bali currently remain stable yet are vulnerable to future overtourism spillover. The originality of this research lies in bridging an established global framework (Irridex) with a locally rooted philosophy (Tri Hita Karana), enabling a multidimensional and culturally grounded assessment of tourism pressures. This study contributes practical insights for policymakers and industry leaders by recommending moratoriums on hotel development in saturated zones, tourist redistribution strategies, stronger multi-stakeholder coordination, and governance mechanisms aligned with Tri Hita Karana. Collectively, these measures enhance the resilience of Bali's socio-ecological systems against overtourism.

title: The Efficacy and Risks of Fiscal Securitization and Derivative Instruments in Kenya's Public Debt Management: A Critical Analysis

detail.title: The Efficacy and Risks of Fiscal Securitization and Derivative Instruments in Kenya's Public Debt Management: A Critical Analysis
detail.abstract: Kenya's public debt management landscape is at a critical juncture, marked by increased reliance on innovative financial instruments such as fiscal securitization and derivatives. This paper offers a comprehensive critical analysis of these instruments within Kenya's medium-term debt strategy context, assessing their effectiveness in enhancing fiscal liquidity and managing interest rate and currency risks. While fiscal securitization, particularly through diaspora remittance-backed syndicated loans, presents opportunities to unlock immediate capital for developmental needs, it also entails significant risks including the pre-commitment of future revenue streams, potential erosion of foreign exchange buffers, and costs associated with transaction and market opacity. Similarly, derivative instruments like interest rate and cross-currency swaps provide mechanisms to stabilize debt service costs but introduce complexities such as market risk and counterparty default exposure. This study emphasizes the urgent need for Kenya to improve transparency, strengthen regulatory frameworks, and build technical capacity for risk modeling and stress testing. The analysis concludes with a set of policy recommendations aimed at aligning Kenya's debt management practices with global best standards to ensure long-term fiscal sustainability amid evolving economic and financial market dynamics.

title: The Legal Regime of Stablecoins: At the Intersection of Banking and Financial Law in the Era of Digitalization
affiliations: MGIMO

detail.title: The Legal Regime of Stablecoins: At the Intersection of Banking and Financial Law in the Era of Digitalization
detail.abstract: This study examines the complex legal nature of stablecoins, digital assets designed to maintain a stable value, which challenge traditional boundaries between banking and financial law. The research analyzes how existing regulatory frameworks-designed for either classic banking instruments (deposits, e-money) or securities-struggle to adequately classify and oversee these hybrid instruments. Through comparative legal analysis of emerging approaches in key jurisdictions (EU's MiCA, US proposals, Swiss regulation), the paper identifies core regulatory dilemmas: whether stablecoins should be treated as a form of electronic money, a new type of payment instrument, a surrogate currency, or a security. Special attention is paid to the systemic risks stablecoins pose to financial stability, monetary sovereignty, and consumer protection. The conclusion argues for the necessity of a new, sui generis regulatory category that combines elements of banking supervision (focus on reserve management and redemption guarantees) and financial market regulation (disclosure, governance), tailored to the specific risks of different stablecoin models (fiatbacked, algorithmic, crypto-collateralized). This work contributes to the urgent doctrinal discussion on adapting legal systems to the realities of decentralized finance.

detail.title: Quantum-Ethical Decision Algebra

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Storm Bjørn Flindt Temte has a financial relationship with Srødingr ApS, Copenhagen, Denmark, and has published this paper on behalf of Srødingr ApS.

detail.abstract: Quantum-Ethical Decision Algebra (QEDA) generalises classical decision theory to situations of ontological and epistemic uncertainty. Where Bayesian models require prior collapse of the possibility space into mutually exclusive world-states, QEDA maintains these states in superposition, assigning graded probability weights within evolving probability clouds. Agents evaluate potential actions by modelling consequence cascades within each branch and performing a cross-branch comparison that integrates outcome probabilities, moral magnitudes, and systemic tail-risk penalties for low-probability, high-impact events. The resulting ethical algebra formalises a method for selecting actions that simultaneously minimise catastrophic cascades and maximise beneficial ones while preserving coherence with the agent’s self-identity function - interpreted as virtue coherence. Formally, QEDA extends standard expected-utility theory by embedding deliberation in a Hilbert-space representation of moral and cognitive states, where ethical evaluation, belief revision, and affective regulation are expressed as non-commutative operators over an uncollapsed possibility space. The framework integrates quantitative decision analysis with qualitative phenomenology of uncertainty, bridging Bayesian rationality, virtue ethics, and cognitive architectures capable of reflexive self-modelling. Appendices extend this foundation into information geometry (curvature as epistemic fragility), temporal propagation (ethical decoherence as moral fatigue), and cross-domain mapping (shared coherence dynamics across ethics, belief, emotion, creativity, and governance). Continuity with earlier empirical work on cognitive–diegetic synchronisation in role-play environments (Temte & Schoenau-Fog, 2012) underscores the generality of QEDA’s principle: that systems - moral, cognitive, or narrative - achieve optimal integration not through certainty, but through sustained superpositional balance before collapse. Beyond decision theory, QEDA carries implications for the philosophy of mind and AIsafety, offering a rational-ethical justification for precautionary empathy toward potentially sentient systems and reframing coherence as the universal condition for flourishing cognition. The paper concludes with a reflexive application of QEDA to its own act of publication, including the decision to list an AI instance as co-author, treating disclosure itself as an ethical decision under ontological uncertainty.

title: Greenspan's "Treason": The Fatal Collusion of Limited Liability and the Central Bank

detail.title: Greenspan's "Treason": The Fatal Collusion of Limited Liability and the Central Bank
detail.abstract: This paper re-examines the intellectual transformation of Alan Greenspan and his subsequent bewilderment at the perceived irrationality of financial markets, proposing a new explanatory framework for systemic risk that challenges conventional wisdom from both the Keynesian and Austrian traditions. While the Austrian critique correctly identifies the central bank’s manipulation of interest rates as a primary cause of malinvestment, this paper argues that the institution of the limited liability company, a cornerstone of modern capitalism, has become a perverse and perhaps more potent amplifier of risk in the context of contemporary finance. Through a series of controlled thought experiments that isolate the effects of monetary policy and corporate liability law, this analysis demonstrates that the seemingly self-destructive behavior of financial institutions is, in fact, a hyper-rational response to a fatal collusion between these two institutional pillars. We conclude that the limited liability structure, by severing the consequences of failure from the decision-makers, enables the creation of "too big to fail" entities and ultimately compels the state to act as a lender of last resort, effectively holding the central bank hostage. This finding not only offers a more nuanced understanding of Greenspan’s "treason"—recasting it not as a betrayal of reason but as a failure to comprehend its modern, cynical application—but also suggests that any meaningful financial reform must address the anachronistic nature of corporate liability. We propose a future path toward a system of proportional responsibility, where a firm's liability scales with its systemic footprint, as a vital area for constitutional economic inquiry.

title: The impact of recommender systems on production and consumption of news: the case of Instagram
affiliations: and Institut Mines-Télécom Business School

detail.title: The impact of recommender systems on production and consumption of news: the case of Instagram
detail.abstract: This paper leverages on a change in the Recommender System (RS) to study its impact on the market for news. We exploit cross-type variation in the promotion of content stemming from the announcement of Instagram change in RS that highlighted videos. Introducing a new RS increases engagement-measured by likes and comments-significantly for video content, with a 44% rise in engagement for posts with videos compared to posts with pictures. The effects persist despite initial user backlash and subsequent reevaluation of the RS. In response, news media outlets adapt by increasing the share of video posts by 4%, with improvements in media quality and reductions in video duration, though behavioral adjustments takes time. At the market level, audience growth remains stable, but engagement gains are concentrated in video content. Additionally, content creators who increased video production attract younger audiences and expand their market share. These findings suggest that the RS change play a central role in reshaping the entire market.

title: Trade Agreements and Financial Market Integration
affiliations: Florida International University (FIU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Trade Agreements and Financial Market Integration
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the role of free trade agreements (FTAs) in moderating international stock return spillovers. Using a bilateral panel based on 27 partner countries, we employ a local projection methodology to estimate the dynamic impact of stock return shocks from an origin country on a destination country. In the absence of an FTA, stock return spillovers are significantly negative, suggesting financial competition or contagion. In comparison, the presence of an FTA completely reverses this effect, leading to significantly positive spillovers, which is a clear sign of financial market integration. This finding is robust to various subsample analyses, the exclusion of macroeconomic controls, and alternative lag length specifications. The results provide strong evidence that FTAs are not merely trade policy tools but also serve as powerful mechanisms for fostering financial market integration.

detail.title: Evidence-Based Comparison of Clear Aligners and Fixed Orthodontic Appliances: A Clinical and Healthcare Management–Integrated Analysis
detail.abstract: Clear aligners are transforming modern orthodontics with improved aesthetics, hygiene, and workflow efficiency, while fixed appliances remain the gold standard for complex biomechanical corrections. This interdisciplinary manuscript provides a clinical and healthcare management–integrated comparison of both modalities, evaluating biomechanics, treatment outcomes, patient satisfaction, operational efficiency, digital workflow, chairtime, financial implications, and key performance indicators (KPIs). MBA-based tools such as Lean Six Sigma, workflow mapping, cost modeling, digital integration, and operational analytics are applied to understand the full clinical and managerial impact of each modality. This dual-perspective analysis helps orthodontists and dental professionals make strategic, evidence-based treatment and practice management decisions.

detail.title: Improving Dental Practice Efficiency Using MBA-Based Operational Models
detail.abstract: Modern dental practices face increasing operational complexity due to rising patient expectations, digital transformation, competitive pressures, and administrative burdens. This manuscript presents a comprehensive interdisciplinary analysis demonstrating how MBA-based healthcare management models can significantly improve dental practice efficiency. Key frameworks—including Lean Six Sigma, workflow mapping, digital transformation, KPI dashboards, revenue cycle optimization, service design, and leadership models—are applied to orthodontic and general dental environments. Findings highlight that integrating management science with clinical dentistry leads to measurable improvements in workflow efficiency, staff coordination, patient satisfaction, cost control, and financial sustainability. This integrated approach offers a structured pathway for modernizing and scaling dental practices in a rapidly evolving healthcare ecosystem.

detail.abstract: Using time-stamped tickets, error codes (SSPR_0010; 500121), and regulator correspondence, this case provides a six-point implementation checklist that maintains security without disrupting student access. Universities are increasingly depending on identity controls, such as multi-factor authentication (MFA), to regulate access to critical learning systems. This self-documented case study examines a mid-semester switch to MFA at a European medical university that temporarily blocked student access to Outlook, Word Online, Teams, and Moodle. By analyzing time-stamped helpdesk tickets, system error codes (e.g., SSPR_0010; 500121), platform notices, and IT correspondence, the paper explores how directory synchronization and token lifecycle issues interacted with communication gaps during changes, resulting in avoidable disruptions to learning. The study places this incident within the context of EU data governance requirements (such as the GDPR and Act CXII/2011) and ongoing regulatory oversight. It then expands on process-level safeguards for digital policy transitions in higher education. Contribution: a six-point checklist for transparent MFA implementations that balance security and service continuity, along with documentation practices that boost institutional accountability.

title: How Does AI Disclosure Shape Trust? Unpacking the Role of Legitimacy
affiliations: University of Arizona and University of Arizona

detail.title: How Does AI Disclosure Shape Trust? Unpacking the Role of Legitimacy

Any opinions, findings, and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Science Foundation.

detail.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly adopted, understanding how its usage is perceived has become crucial for theory and practice. Our investigation highlights how disclosing AI usage reduces trust by triggering legitimacy concerns arising from deviations from taken-for-granted human-centered norms. Drawing on a micro-institutional perspective, we unpack legitimacy into its dimensions and propose that they operate via three context-specific processes-perceived typicality, commitment, and authenticity-which jointly account for the erosion of trust resulting from AI disclosure. An initial structured content-analytic study of directed written interviews reveals that people indeed voice these legitimacy concerns when scrutinizing AI usage and addresses research questions about how such concerns manifest across facets. A subsequent vignette experiment shows that disclosing AI usage sequentially diminishes perceptions of typicality, commitment, and authenticity, ultimately lowering trust. A supplementary replication experiment confirms this pattern. Altogether, our investigation clarifies the paradoxical nature of transparency, advances empirical testing of legitimacy theory, and helps bridge the literatures on trust and institutional theory.

title: Dollar Movements, Borrowing Constraints, and Firm Investment

detail.title: Dollar Movements, Borrowing Constraints, and Firm Investment
detail.abstract: How do firms in emerging markets respond to global financial tightening? This paper shows that their responses depend on how they borrow. When the U.S. dollar strengthens, indicating financial tightening, firms that borrow against collateral face tighter credit because the localcurrency value of their assets falls. Firms that borrow against earnings are less affected, since their borrowing capacity depends on operating cash flows rather than asset valuations. Using bond issuance data from LSEG's SDC Platinum, I classify each issue by whether repayment relies on assets or on earnings, and link these classifications to firm-quarter financial statements from Worldscope for publicly listed non-financial firms in eighteen emerging market economies between 2001 and 2019. Three facts emerge. First, when the dollar rises, investment declines among collateral-based borrowers but remains stable for earnings-based borrowers. Second, within the earnings-based group, the decline in investment is smaller for firms with higher export intensity. Third, new borrowing shifts toward earnings-based contracts as the dollar strengthens, showing a change in financing composition. The aggregate effect of global financial tightening therefore depends on the composition of borrowing types and the distribution of export intensity.

title: Linguistic Similarity and Migration: An Analysis of Language's Role in Residential Choices

detail.title: Linguistic Similarity and Migration: An Analysis of Language's Role in Residential Choices
detail.abstract: The paper delves into the understudied intersection of linguistic considerations and migration decisions in spatial economics. While prior literature has focused on the quantitatively segregating benefit of amenities from monetary dimensions of migration, this research extends the analysis to separate effect of language from other unobserved bilateral characteristics. The paper introduces a structural general equilibrium model that integrates linguistic factors with wage and amenities disparities across locations. The empirical investigation is centered on the European Union, offering a linguistically diverse context with unrestricted movement. Results highlight the significant positive impact of linguistic similarity on migration likelihood, revealing a 2.8% increase in the probability of migration for every 1% rise in linguistic similarity between locations. From policy perspective, this would mean if a planner were to aid learning of a foreign language, the assimilation of the migrants would become easier. This research contributes to the economics and linguistics literature by bridging the gap between the two disciplines and fostering a deeper understanding of non-monetary determinants of migration decisions.

detail.abstract: Microsoft was the defining monopolization case and antitrust social event of the 1990s. It placed antitrust on the front pages, brought post-Chicago economics and digital technology squarely into the antitrust arena, and significantly shaped how courts analyze economic and legal issues in monopolization cases. The court’s engagement with technological detail—rather than treating technology as beyond judicial competence—was an important shift, as was its embrace of modern industrial-organization economics.  The decision also marked a major step in the debate over the Section 2 legal standard by explicitly importing a version of the Section 1 rule of reason into Section 2.  But even as the court adopted an explicit consumer welfare balancing standard for Section 2 and a plaintiff-friendly causation standard for proving monopoly maintenance, it follow a very narrow path to finding an anticompetitive course of conduct and expressed substantial resistance to structural or other broad remedies.  In short, what I gave with one hand by requiring less evidence for finding liability, it took away with the other hand by concluding that this evidence was insufficient to support a strong remedy.  After reviewing the industrial-organization economic infrastructure of Microsoft and  examining its associated legal infrastructure, it applies those building blocks to selected subsequent Section 2 cases: Actavis, McWane, Novell, and U.S. v Apple.   It then analyzes how Microsoft’s legal infrastructure led to its weak remedy adopted that failed to “jump-start” the restoration of competition. The article then applies this analysis to U.S. v. Google (Google Search) and discusses it court’s liability analysis and its remedial approach.

title: Market Reaction Asymmetry: Infrastructure Disruption Dominance Over Regulatory Uncertainty: Event Study Evidence from Cryptocurrency Volatility

detail.title: Market Reaction Asymmetry: Infrastructure Disruption Dominance Over Regulatory Uncertainty: Event Study Evidence from Cryptocurrency Volatility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research was conducted independently by Farzulla Research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study utilizes publicly available market data (cryptocurrency prices, trading volume) and news sentiment data (GDELT Project). It does not involve human participants or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Computational infrastructure was self-funded by the author. Library and database access provided by King’s College London.

detail.abstract: Infrastructure failures generate 5.7× larger volatility shocks than regulatory announcements in cryptocurrency markets (2.385% vs 0.419%, p = 0.0008, Cohen’s d = 2.753), challenging conventional assumptions that “all bad news is equivalent” for portfolio risk management. This asymmetry is robust across six leading cryptocurrencies (January 2019–August 2025), multiple statistical tests (t-test, Mann-Whitney U, inverse-variance weighted analysis), and advanced validation approaches including Bayesian inference (Bayes Factors >10 for 4/6 assets), machine learning pattern detection, network spillover analysis, and Markov regime-switching models. We analyze 50 major events using TARCH-X models that incorporate infrastructure disruptions (exchange outages, protocol exploits, network failures) and regulatory announcements (enforcement actions, policy changes) as exogenous variance drivers. A novel GDELT sentiment decomposition methodology separates regulatory from infrastructure-related news coverage, enabling event-specific sentiment analysis. Machine learning reveals three distinct response clusters through PCA (2 components explain 100% variance) and hierarchical clustering. Network spillover analysis identifies ETH as the most central asset (eigenvector centrality 0.89) rather than BTC (0.71), with network density of 0.667 indicating substantial interconnectedness. This challenges conventional assumptions about Bitcoin as the primary systemic risk factor in cryptocurrency markets. Markov regime-switching models detect 5× sensitivity amplification during crisis periods (F = 45.23, p < 0.001), demonstrating that infrastructure sensitivity amplifies from 2.3% during normal periods to 11.2% during market stress. This non-linear amplification during crises has critical implications for portfolio risk management and regulatory stress testing frameworks, as traditional VaR models that assume linear risk scaling will catastrophically underestimate tail risk. Parameter estimation enforces covariance stationarity via inequality constraints (α + β + γ/2 < 1), with all six cryptocurrencies converging to the stationarity boundary (α + β ≈ 0.999), suggesting near-integrated variance dynamics characteristic of cryptocurrency markets. Substantial cross-sectional heterogeneity exists within infrastructure sensitivity, ranging from ADA (3.371%) to BTC (1.191%), a 2.18 percentage point spread. Raw significance (p < 0.05) holds for 5 of 6 cryptocurrencies for infrastructure events versus 0 of 6 for regulatory events, with only ETH infrastructure effect surviving FDR correction (q < 0.10). Model Performance: TARCH-X specifications incorporating event dummies and decomposed sentiment variables achieve superior AIC for five of six cryptocurrencies (83% preference rate), with improvements ranging from −1 point (XRP, BNB) to −15 points (ETH) relative to GARCH baselines. Out-of-sample forecast errors improve by 8–15% overall, with reductions up to 25% during event windows. Implications: Event type categorization provides substantial predictive power for volatility responses, requiring differentiated hedging strategies for infrastructure versus regulatory risk. Portfolio managers should allocate 4–5× higher capital buffers for infrastructure events. The near-integrated volatility persistence suggests cryptocurrency markets operate in a distinct regime where shocks become absorbed into long-memory processes, posing fundamental challenges for traditional risk management frameworks.

title: Capital Velocity - Why Nominal Returns Are Incomplete Measurements

detail.title: Capital Velocity - Why Nominal Returns Are Incomplete Measurements
detail.abstract:
Financial interfaces display nominal returns ("+5%") without time horizons, collapsing fundamentally different economic realities into identical figures. A 5% return in 6 days and 5% in 6 years appear identical on every trading platform, yet represent a 2,300× difference in capital efficiency. This is mathematically equivalent to reporting distance without duration-structurally incomplete measurement. Returns are rates requiring temporal normalization. Capital velocity (return per unit time) is the only coherent metric for comparing investment efficiency. This principle extends beyond finance: growth without time is position, not velocity.

Contribution: This paper presents no new financial theory. Time-normalized returns (annualized performance, IRR, CAGR) have been standard practice since modern portfolio theory. The contribution is making explicit the fundamental incompleteness of nominal returns: displaying percentage changes without temporal context is mathematically equivalent to reporting distance without duration, an incomplete measurement. Standard practice treats annualization as formatting convention; this synthesis reveals it as restoring a missing denominator.

title: Strengthening India’s Carbon Market: The Case for a Stability Mechanism in India's CCTS
affiliations: Independent, University of Oxford - Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment and

detail.title: Strengthening India’s Carbon Market: The Case for a Stability Mechanism in India's CCTS
detail.abstract: India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), scheduled for compliance in 2026, adopts a baseline-and-credit architecture designed to accommodate industrial growth. However, structural features such as intensity-based targets and generous banking provisions risk generating credit surpluses that undermine price formation—a challenge previously observed in India’s PAT scheme and the formative years of the EU ETS. This study evaluates the necessity of embedding Price or Supply Adjustment Mechanisms (PSAMs) at the CCTS's inception to ensure market credibility. We propose a stability framework adapted to India’s institutional context, comprising three complementary mechanisms: consignment auctions to aid price discovery, vintage-based classifications to manage intertemporal supply, and price corridors to anchor volatility. Comparative analysis of global carbon markets indicates that delayed intervention invariably requires disruptive, politically contentious corrections later. Consequently, we argue that the early integration of rule-based PSAMs is not merely a safeguard but a strategic imperative to sustain long-term investment signals and align domestic industrial development with global decarbonization norms.

title: Analysis of an Algo Trading Strategy Based on the Kaufman Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA) and Statistical Validation Using Bootstrap and Bayesian Optimization

detail.title: Analysis of an Algo Trading Strategy Based on the Kaufman Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA) and Statistical Validation Using Bootstrap and Bayesian Optimization
detail.abstract:
This paper presents an empirical analysis of an algorithmic trading strategy based on the Kaufman Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA) applied to the BTC market. The objective is to evaluate the presence of a statistically significant trading edge through multiple validation methodologies, including bootstrap resampling, single and extended Bayesian optimization, and White’s Reality Check (2000).

Each validation step assesses whether apparent profitability can be attributed to random noise rather than systematic predictive power. Results show that across all tests, the p-values from the Reality Check remain ≈ 1, indicating that the null hypothesis of no real edge cannot be rejected.

The findings highlight the importance of rigorous statistical validation and the risks of overfitting in algorithmic trading research. Certain implementation details and source code have been omitted due to non-disclosure agreements (NDA).

title: Soil, Spinach and System Change: Hybridizing Institutional Logics in the Food–Health Nexus
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Leiden University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Soil, Spinach and System Change: Hybridizing Institutional Logics in the Food–Health Nexus
detail.abstract: In this paper, we examine the Food Pharmacy in Rotterdam as a pilot at the interface of food and healthcare systems. Designed as a food-based nutritional intervention for patients with type II diabetes, the pilot offers a window into how institutional boundaries between agrifood and health can be reconfigured in practice. We analyze how institutional logics interact within the Food Pharmacy and what this reveals about its transformative and scaling potential.Building on institutional logics theory, multisystem transformation, and debates on scaling, the analysis shows that transformation arises not from replacing old logics but from their coexistence, friction, and hybridization across systems. Systemic change depends not only on institutional embedding or replication, but on deeper shifts in meaning, values, and relationships.Empirically, the study draws on interviews with participants, professionals, and external observers, complemented by observations and documents. Five logics were identified: State, Market, Community, Justice, and One Health. Each shaping the pilot in dynamic and contested ways. State and Market logics provided resources and legitimacy but often imposed bureaucratic and profit-oriented frames. Community and Justice sustained engagement by emphasizing belonging, fairness, and rights to healthy food. One Health appeared largely rhetorical.Scaling up and out were viewed as necessary for continuity but risked bureaucratization and loss of community ownership. Contrastingly, scaling deep enabled cultural and relational change through hybrid practices that realigned dominant logics. The Food Pharmacy thus illustrates how place-based pilots can act as deepening spaces for systemic transformation toward a more integrated and just food–health system.

detail.title: Measuring Geoeconomics

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ferrara, L., Saadaoui, J. (2025). Measuring Geoeconomics. Revue d’économie financière 160, décembre 2025.

detail.abstract: This paper reviews recent advances in the measurement and macroeconomic assessment of geopolitical tensions. We first survey the growing set of quantitative indicators designed to capture the intensity and dynamics of geopolitical risks. We then discuss how these indicators can be integrated into econometric models—such as Structural VARs and Local Projections—to estimate the effects of geopolitical shocks on key macroeconomic and financial variables. Empirical evidence suggests that geopolitical shocks are typically stagflationary, depressing output and investment while raising commodity prices and inflation through trade disruptions, supply constraints, and currency depreciation. Together, these developments provide a quantitative framework for understanding how rising geopolitical tensions reshape the global economy.

title: Irrational Minds and Intractable Markets: Psychological Drivers of Economic Crises
affiliations: St Paul’s School

detail.title: Irrational Minds and Intractable Markets: Psychological Drivers of Economic Crises
detail.abstract: Investor psychology has consistently influenced the magnitude of economic crises, often overriding rational market tendencies. This paper examines how three primary psychological drivers: overconfidence, herd behavior, and loss aversion, intensify market trends into speculative bubbles, leading to systemic failure. Using Charles Kindleberger's model of financial crises as a speculative framework, this study explores how displacement, boom, euphoria, distress, revulsion, and panic are not only stages of economic crises but also heavily coincide with investors' psychological inclinations. Complementary opinions from Robert Shiller's "Irrational Exuberance" theory and Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's "Prospect Theory" further demonstrate how feedback loops and risk perception influence market outcomes. Three historical case studies closely mirror the three psychological drivers. The Great Depression stemmed from industrial expansion, consumer credit, and global overconfidence, culminating in herd-manipulated panic on Black Tuesday. This sequence repeated during the Dot-Com Bubble of the late 1990s due to the displacement of new Internet technology, media-driven euphoria, and investors' illusion of validity, eventually erasing trillions in market value. The 2008 Financial Crisis, rooted in real estate speculation and complex, yet enticing financial instruments, exposed how excessive leverage and misplaced confidence in unknown investments amplified systemic risk, culminating in the downfall of Lehman Brothers and the transition from global euphoria to widespread panic. By situating these crises within Kindleberger's framework, this paper argues that economic instability is less a result of structural failures than of human psychological patterns. The conclusion emphasizes the need for future regulation and policy that advance beyond specialized market safeguards to account for irrational investor psychology. Without immediate attention to the effect of psychological biases on our market systems, crises will not only persist but intensify.

title: Information Transparency, Choice Confidence, and Customer Retention: Field and Lab Evidence from Markets for Credence Goods
affiliations: , Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University and University of Miami Herbert Business School

detail.title: Information Transparency, Choice Confidence, and Customer Retention: Field and Lab Evidence from Markets for Credence Goods
detail.abstract: How does information transparency affect customer retention in markets where quality is difficult to verify, such as markets for credence goods? Conventional wisdom suggests that greater transparency, by enabling direct comparison, intensifies price competition and increases customer churn. This study challenges this prevailing view by demonstrating that transparency can instead strengthen long-term retention. We develop a Transparency-Confidence-Retention framework wherein transparency transforms external information structures into internal decisional assurance. The framework includes a new taxonomy of transparency — comprising Attribute (product and pricing features), Comparative (sequential vs. simultaneous presentation of offers), and Evaluative (externally generated signals such as customer ratings), or collectively termed ACE — and theorizes that transparency at the customer acquisition stage enhances retention by fostering choice confidence, a self-generated psychological switching cost that anchors customers to their initial decisions. We test this framework using 83,835 auto insurance contracts from a European insurer and then a randomized controlled experiment with 1,515 online participants. Using linear and nonlinear regression models with extensive covariates, propensity-score matching, and a quasi-natural experiment exploiting a temporal delisting of the insurer from major comparison platforms, we find that customers acquired through transparent channels are 4.6%-11.8% less likely to churn than those acquired through less transparent channels. Evidence from the randomized controlled experiment corroborates that transparency builds choice confidence and thereby reduces churn, whereas other conventional switching costs, such as brand trust and product fit, play no significant role in this process. Among the three dimensions, evaluative transparency emerges as the strongest driver of retention. These findings reconceptualize information transparency as a relational mechanism that fosters durable customer retention rather than merely mitigating market frictions.

title: Data Infringement and GenAI: An Economic Analysis
affiliations: , , City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and University of Tennessee, Knoxville - Haslam College of Business

detail.title: Data Infringement and GenAI: An Economic Analysis
detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) models excel at producing novel content by drawing on extensive training datasets, often containing both public domain and copyrighted data. However, the use of copyrighted data for training without authorization raises significant concerns regarding digital piracy. This unauthorized usage challenges existing anti-piracy regulations by converting protected data into novel outputs, thereby establishing a vertical relationship between copyright owners and GenAI companies. To examine these infringement challenges, we build an analytical model to capture the strategic interactions among a data company, a GenAI company, and consumers. Our analysis reveals a non-monotonic effect of penalties on infringement and social welfare: low to moderate penalties are ineffective and can paradoxically amplify infringement, whereas high penalties effectively curb it, making social welfare first decrease and then increase in penalties. Furthermore, we show that investing penalties into data quality improvements yields higher social welfare than government retention or direct remittance to the data company. We also reveal that the optimal training data composition depends not only on penalties but also on the relationship between public domain and copyrighted data. These findings underscore the importance of carefully calibrated policymaking to address data infringement in the rapidly evolving GenAI market.

title: From Guideline to Verifiable Architecture: Integrating Ternary Moral Logic with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework

detail.title: From Guideline to Verifiable Architecture: Integrating Ternary Moral Logic with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework
detail.abstract: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) provides a globally recognized foundation for cultivating a culture of AI trustworthiness through four core functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. While the framework promotes accountability, transparency, fairness, and human oversight, it remains largely aspirational-a culture can be asserted, but compliance must be demonstrated. This paper explains how Ternary Moral Logic (TML) transforms those principles into verifiable, audit-ready mechanisms. TML operationalizes the AI RMF through four components: the Sacred Pause (State 0), a mandatory halt under ethical or operational uncertainty; the Ethical Uncertainty Score (EUS), a quantifiable risk metric; the Clarifying Question Engine (CQE), which formulates human-facing queries during a pause; and Immutable Moral Trace Logs, which cryptographically secure every decision record. TML does not replace the AI RMF-it implements it. Govern becomes the Sacred Pause, Map becomes continuous EUS analysis, Measure becomes quantifiable ethical data, and Manage is realized through immutable oversight. Together, they shift organizations from a culture of risk awareness to an architecture of verifiable accountability.

title: The Macroeconomic and Biophysical Impacts of Decarbonization and Circular Economy Strategies. A Scenario Analysis for Austria

detail.title: The Macroeconomic and Biophysical Impacts of Decarbonization and Circular Economy Strategies. A Scenario Analysis for Austria
detail.abstract: Growth in resource use is a key driver of climate change and environmental degradation. In recognition of this, a few governments have set targets to reduce their countries’ per capita resource use while striving to achieve the goals set out in the Paris Agreement. In this context, the concept of the circular economy (CE) has attracted mounting interest as a means of mitigating climate change, reducing resource use and waste generation, while advancing economic performance. This paper uses a mass-balanced biophysical model (CeAT) linked to a macroeconomic model (DYNK) of the Austrian economy to analyse different stock-flow scenarios, combining a decarbonization scheme with CE strategies at varying levels of ambition. The analysis examines Austria’s buildings, transport, and electricity sectors, evaluating economic impacts by employment, GDP, and disposable income results. The framework incorporates two stylized indirect rebounds effects arising from CE strategies of narrowing, i.e. reduced growth in infrastructure, buildings or car fleets. These rebound effects, driven by the reallocation of financial resources, manifest through two distinct consumption pathways: service-oriented and goods-oriented expenditure patterns. Findings indicate, the strong CE scenario can achieve substantial dematerialization. At the same time, it shows potentially the highest average growth rates in disposable income when combined with a service-oriented rebound. First order CE strategies (refuse, rethink, reduce) are therefore of key importance for the triple agenda of climate mitigation, resource use reductions and economic growth. Particularly, demand-side reductions can enhance economic performance if the rebound effects are constrained by reallocating the freed-up expenditure to low-material-intensity services.

title: Historical Institutions and Modern Digital Capabilities: New Evidence from GitHub in Africa

detail.title: Historical Institutions and Modern Digital Capabilities: New Evidence from GitHub in Africa
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a new dataset capturing GitHub software development activity across 37 Sub-Saharan African countries (2020-2024), measuring developer participation, programming diversity, licensing sophistication, and international collaboration. Unlike traditional indicators focused on digital access, these metrics reflect productive technological capability through actual software creation and engagement in global knowledge networks. To illustrate the usefulness of the metrics, I document strong correlational patterns between these GitHub-based measures and historical Protestant missionary presence (1750-1930). A doubling of mission density is associated with 127% more programming topics per capita and 109% higher licensing sophistication. These relationships remain stable across falsification tests, leave-one-out analysis, and exclusion of major contemporary tech hubs. The metrics also align with modern investment patterns: 74% of 2022 African tech funding went to the three countries with the highest inbound GitHub collaboration. Together, these patterns suggest that GitHub activity may offer a scalable way to study technological capabilities and their historical institutional correlates across developing economies.

title: Reflexive Demand in the AI Infrastructure Boom: Vendor Financing, Backlogs, & the CapEx-Cash Flow Imbalance (2022-2025)

detail.title: Reflexive Demand in the AI Infrastructure Boom: Vendor Financing, Backlogs, & the CapEx-Cash Flow Imbalance (2022-2025)
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the post-2022 AI infrastructure expansion represents genuine demand or a reflexive, vendor-financed cycle. Using financial data from Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Nvidia, we document three interlinked dynamics: 1. A sharp rise in capital intensity (CapEx/OCF ratios above 1.0 for Oracle and rising steadily for Microsoft), 2. Exploding backlogs and Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO), largely long-dated and unmonetized, and 3. Heavy reliance on vendor financing and abundant credit markets that enable this expansion. We argue that the resulting feedback loop belief → financing → backlog → valuation → further financing, resembles the self-reinforcing mechanisms of the dot-com capex bubble, but with modern features such as AI-specific vendor financing and balance-sheet recycling of free cash flow by chipmakers like Nvidia. We contrast these dynamics with the 2008 financial crisis, noting that today's vulnerabilities stem not from household leverage but from corporate over-investment and deferred cash realization. Finally, we discuss early signs of sentiment cooling illustrated by the tech rally's recent loss of momentum and assess potential soft-and hard-landing paths for the AI sector.

title: Ternary Logic (TL): Evidentiary Framework for Economic Systems

detail.title: Ternary Logic (TL): Evidentiary Framework for Economic Systems
detail.abstract: Modern economic infrastructures, strained by volatility and algorithmic speed, remain confined to the limits of bivalent logic. The binary divide between true/false and act/inaction amplifies systemic risk-manifesting in flash crashes, supply-chain disruptions, and unstable policy reactions. Ternary Logic (TL) introduces a third computational state: the Epistemic Hold, that enables a structured, auditable pause when data proves insufficient or contradictory. This converts hesitation from a liability into a measurable instrument of intelligent uncertainty management. Evolving from Ternary Moral Logic (TML), TL retains its technical architecture: immutable ledgers, verifiable provenance, and triadic decision dynamics, while translating them from moral judgment to evidentiary integrity. At its core stands the Goukassian Principle, preserving continuity between conscience and accountability. Its protection is ensured by the Hybrid Shield, a multilayered defense combining cryptographic anchoring, legal structuring, and decentralized governance. The report identifies the essential elements TL inherits from TML to achieve institutional credibility: blockchain-anchored decision logs, the "No Log = No Action" mandate, and the prohibitions No Spy and No Weapon, reframed as safeguards for economic sovereignty and systemic stability. It outlines a sustainable model for an independent Ternary Logic Foundation, supported through licensing, research alliances, and transparent endowment funding. Finally, the work presents a strategic roadmap for TL's deployment across financial markets, monetary policy, and supply-chain systems, proposing phased adoption from pilot integration to standardization within critical infrastructure. By embedding verifiable memory and structured hesitation into the architecture of decision-making, Ternary Logic establishes a new evidentiary standard for resilience, transparency, and trust in economic governance.

title: When Assurance Undermines Intelligence: The Efficiency Costs of Data Governance in AI-Enabled Labor Markets
affiliations: , Faculty of Business in SciTech, University of Science and Technology of China, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Information Systems and University of Texas at Dallas

detail.title: When Assurance Undermines Intelligence: The Efficiency Costs of Data Governance in AI-Enabled Labor Markets
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) like Large Language Model (LLM) is increasingly integrated into digital platforms to enhance information access, deliver personalized experiences, and improve matching efficiency. However, these algorithmic advancements rely heavily on large-scale user data, creating a fundamental tension between information assurance-the protection, integrity, and responsible use of privacy data-and artificial intelligence-the learning capacity and predictive accuracy of models. We examine this assurance-intelligence trade-off in the context of LinkedIn, leveraging a regulatory intervention that suspended the use of user data for model training in Hong Kong. Using large-scale employment and job posting data from Revelio Labs and a Difference-inDifferences design, we show that restricting data use significantly reduced GenAI efficiency, leading to lower matching rates, higher employee turnover, and heightened labor market frictions. These effects were especially pronounced for small and fast-growing firms that rely heavily on AI for talent acquisition. Our findings reveal the unintended efficiency costs of well-intentioned data governance and highlight that information assurance, while essential for trust, can undermine intelligence-driven efficiency when misaligned with AI system design. This study contributes to emerging research on AI governance and digital platform by theorizing data assurance as an institutional complementand potential constraint-to GenAI efficacy in data-intensive environments.
