detail.title: The Impacts of Guaranteed Basic Income on Crime Perpetration and Victimization

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper provides the first experimental evidence on the impact of providing a guaranteed basic income on criminal perpetration and victimization. We analyze a nationwide randomized controlled trial that provided 2,000 unemployed individuals in Finland with an unconditional monthly payment of 560 Euros for two years (2017-2018), while 173,222 comparable individuals remained under the existing social safety net. Using comprehensive administrative data on police reports and district court trials, we estimate precise zero effects on criminal perpetration and victimization. Point estimates are small and statistically insignificant across all crime categories. Our confidence intervals rule out reductions in perpetration of 5 percent or more for crime reports and 10 percent or more for criminal charges.

detail.title: Redefining Challenges Based on Emergent Gameplay
detail.abstract: This article aims to explore the limitations of traditional game challenge models in explaining modern games characterized by emergent gameplay. Using Don't Starve as a case study, this research analyzes its challenge design and finds that traditional models struggle to adequately describe two types of phenomena: first, challenges dynamically triggered by the player's own attributes (such as sanity); second, emergent solutions created by players exploiting the rules of the game's ecosystem (such as directing hostile creatures into combat). Based on these findings, this article proposes extensions to the traditional challenge model: adding an "attribute-influence" property to challenge objects and revising the definition of "helper" property to encompass persistent effects and dynamic changes, with cases demonstrating their practical applications. This research suggests that to adapt to the complexity of open-world games, challenge models must move beyond the traditional "puzzle" framework by incorporating the dynamic relationship between player attributes and challenge objects, while also considering the impact of new challenge types on the overall gaming experience.

detail.abstract: Renewable energy system decentralisation requires intelligent, transparent and secure energy generation, transmission, distribution, and trading approaches. This study focuses on the role of artificial intelligence and blockchain technology in enhancing the concept of decentralised renewable energy trading through the reduction of inefficiencies, data ignorance, and trust challenges found in conventional power systems. Artificial intelligence predictive algorithms are used to optimise energy consumption and distribution, and the blockchain immutable registry keeps the integrity, transparency and responsibility of transactions. Collectively, these technologies support the creation of a decent and reliable digital energy market. The study reviewed case studies and related studies from African as well as other global environments to investigate the adoption patterns and infrastructural constraints, and regulatory preparedness in influencing the adoption of these technologies. The findings reveal that artificial intelligence and blockchain technology can significantly enhance the energy efficiency and market transparency but the holistic deployment of the technology remains limited with weak digital infrastructure, limited stakeholder awareness, and regulatory uncertainties. The study recommends a well robust harmonised policy and technical solution, which involves focused investments, regional coordination and institutional capacity building to achieve an equitable decarbonisation. detail.abstract: Digital financial inclusion (DFI) has emerged as a critical driver of productivity, competitiveness, and resilience among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Sub-Saharan Africa. As mobile technology reshapes access to finance, new opportunities are opening for previously excluded entrepreneurs to integrate into regional and global markets. This paper examines how digital financial inclusion strengthens SME competitiveness through access to digital payments, credit, and savings instruments, while also exploring policy and infrastructure challenges that limit its full potential. Drawing on evidence from Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana, the analysis highlights the importance of digital ecosystems, regulatory frameworks, and gender-responsive innovation. The study concludes that digital financial inclusion, if effectively governed, can serve as a cornerstone for inclusive industrial growth and regional economic integration in Africa.

title: Delivering Higher Pay? The Impacts of a Task-Level Pay Standard in the Gig Economy
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University, Carnegie Mellon University and Carnegie Mellon University - H. John Heinz III School of Public Policy and Management

detail.title: Delivering Higher Pay? The Impacts of a Task-Level Pay Standard in the Gig Economy

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
How does a task-level minimum pay requirement for gig workers affect their earnings and employment? We study this question in the context of a January 2024 law in Seattle that establishes a per-task minimum pay standard for app-based delivery workers. Drawing on novel cross-platform, trip-level gig activity data, we compare earnings and employment trajectories around the implementation of the law for workers who were doing delivery work in Seattle before the reform against workers who had been active in other regions of Washington State. We find that the minimum pay law raised delivery pay per task, though the increases in base pay per task were partially offset by a substantial reduction in average tips, a major component of delivery pay. At the same time, the policy led to a reduction in the number of tasks completed by highly attached incumbent drivers (but not an increase in exit from delivery work), completely offsetting increased pay per task and leading to zero effect on monthly earnings. We find evidence that drivers experienced more unpaid idle time and longer distances driven between tasks, but find no evidence that drivers reduced their total time working on delivery apps and only limited evidence of switching from delivery to ride-hailing work. Using a simple model of the labor market for platform delivery drivers, we show that our evidence is consistent with free entry of drivers into the delivery market driving down the task-finding rate until expected earnings return to their pre-reform level. These findings highlight the challenges of raising pay in spot markets for tasks where there is free entry of workers.

detail.abstract: The interplay between basic survival pressures and higher-order psychological needs remains undertheorized in social science. In this paper, I introduce Red Line Theory, a framework that integrates biological limits, existential thresholds, and adaptive capacity to explain both individual collapse and social upheaval. The theory delineates three central constructs: the Objective Red Line-the non-negotiable material conditions required for survival; the Subjective Red Line-the minimal acceptable conditions for dignity, meaning, and psychological endurance; and Adaptability-the capacity to buffer, shift, or temporarily sustain these thresholds. Situated within holistic and existential thought, the framework extends beyond classical need and deprivation models such as Maslow's hierarchy and relative deprivation theory. When objective conditions fall below biological necessity, physical survival is endangered; when perceived conditions drop beneath the subjective minimum, psychological breakdown or collective revolt becomes likely. Adaptability moderates these dynamics, temporarily averting collapse. The theory explains diverse phenomena-mental disorders, revolutionary movements, and social instability-more comprehensively than one-dimensional models and suggests empirical pathways for operationalization, including survival indices, dignity surveys, and resilience metrics. Red Line Theory thus provides a unified dual-threshold model of human behavior under pressure, bridging physiological necessity and existential purpose. It offers a rigorous yet integrative perspective for understanding stability and crisis across both individual and societal levels.

title: Data-Driven Innovation And Privacy Concerns In A Schumpeterian Growth Model

detail.title: Data-Driven Innovation And Privacy Concerns In A Schumpeterian Growth Model

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Auckland Business School Research Paper (forthcoming)

detail.abstract: This paper develops a Schumpeterian growth model in which consumer data are used as the R&D input for quality improvements, and consumers balance the economic benefits of selling their consumption data against privacy concerns. In the market equilibrium, a higher degree of privacy concerns reduces the supply of consumer data, hindering innovation and thereby slowing down growth. This finding is consistent with our crosscountry empirical evidence that privacy concerns are negatively correlated with regional digital development. Furthermore, our model shows that if the degree of privacy concerns exceeds a certain threshold, the decentralized equilibrium features socially excessive innovation, suggesting that data use should be more strictly regulated or taxed. In contrast, if the degree of privacy concerns is lower than this threshold value, innovation in the decentralized equilibrium is below the socially efficient level, and policies that promote or subsidize data use become socially desirable. These findings help us understand crosscountry differences in data regulation policies.

title: The Economics of Socio-Ecological Transformations. A conceptual framework

detail.title: The Economics of Socio-Ecological Transformations. A conceptual framework
detail.abstract: The paper introduces the SETER framework, a conceptual tool for analyzing the interplay between Socio-Ecological Transformation (SET) and Economic Reasoning (ER). In the context of global crises and the contested nature of sustainability discourses, the framework identifies nine key categories – ranging from economic goals and the role of the state to transformative dynamics and agency – to systematically compare diverse SET narratives and their basic underlying economic assumptions. Drawing on insights from Social Studies of Economics (SSE) and Sustainability Transitions Research (STR), the framework highlights how ER shapes SET discourses and potential pathways, influencing both the diagnosis of socio-ecological crises and its proposed solutions. The paper applies the framework for two contrasting cases: the EU Green Deal, which exemplifies a market-driven “green growth” narrative, and Kōhei Saitō’s Degrowth Manifesto, which advocates for commons-based, sufficiency-orientated transformation. These cases illustrate the framework’s ability to map competing visions of SET, revealing the systemic dependencies between ER categories and their manifestations. The SETER framework also enables a typification of antagonistic narratives opposing SET, such as techno-libertarian or fossil-modernization discourses. While the framework provides a useful tool for categorising and comparing SET narratives, its integration with power-focused analytical tools is necessary to assess the performative influence of these narratives. By offering a flexible, cross-sectoral, and longitudinal approach, the SETER framework provides a robust methodology for navigating the complexities of SET-related discourses, current counter-developments, and the critical role of economic imaginaries.

title: Environmental and economic effects of pay-as-you-throw waste taxation: an assessment based on difference-in-differences models

detail.title: Environmental and economic effects of pay-as-you-throw waste taxation: an assessment based on difference-in-differences models
detail.abstract: Excessive municipal waste generation remains a pressing environmental challenge in the European Union, motivating the adoption of policies such as Pay-As-You-Throw (PAYT) schemes that link household waste management fees to unsorted waste production. Rigorous evaluation of PAYT’s effects is complicated by staggered policy adoption and non-reliable parallel trends across municipalities, which can bias standard Difference-in-Differences (DiD) estimates. We address this challenge by comparing two-way fixed effects DiD, staggered DiD, and Synthetic DiD (SDID) approaches. Applying this framework to the staggered PAYT rollout in the Italian region of Emilia-Romagna, we find a robust 10% increase in sorted waste collection rates on average. This shift is almost entirely due to a reduction of unsorted waste per capita, without a significant growth of sorted waste generated, aligning to the top priority of the EU Waste Hierarchy, i.e. waste prevention. Importantly, PAYT does not significantly raise the total cost of the waste management service on average, although it does involve a shift in the composition of cost components. Thus, the study underscores the potential of PAYT as an economically viable policy instrument for municipalities and regions to advance urban waste management in line with circular economy objectives.

detail.abstract: This study proposes "generalized homothetic robust Epstein-Zin (GHREZ) utility," in which the coefficient of relative ambiguity aversion in homothetic robust Epstein-Zin (HREZ) utility is generalized to a positive-definite matrix of relative ambiguity aversions. We analyze a robust consumptioninvestment problem with GHREZ utility under a quadratic security market model. We demonstrate that the volatility of the optimal robust portfolio can be expressed as a weighted average of the market price of risk and the "investor hedging value of intertemporal uncertainty." We derive an approximate optimal robust portfolio and quantitatively analyze the relationship between the approximate optimal robust portfolios and relative ambiguity aversion matrices. Numerical analysis reveals that as deviations from the relative ambiguity aversion matrix under HREZ utility increase, deviations from the approximate optimal asset allocation under HREZ utility also increase, and the sensitivity is significant. This finding suggests that GHREZ utility is promising for solving the equity home bias puzzle.

title: Quasi-Judicial: A History and Tradition
affiliations: Yale Law School and Boston University - School of Law

detail.title: Quasi-Judicial: A History and Tradition
detail.abstract:
In challenging the historical assumptions underlying the unitary executive theory, scholars have made several seemingly unrelated discoveries. First, "judicial" power was conceived in English law as a subset of "executive" authority. Second, Congress at or near the Founding insulated certain court-like comissions from presidential control. Finally, the "quasi-judicial" and "quasi-legislative" powers that were central to the holding of Humphrey's Executor flowed from a forgotten nineteenth-century legal tradition was guiding Congress's construction of the modern state. This Essay connects these findings into a single claim: generations of American stretching back past the Founding have instinctively insulated administrators granted quasi-judicial functions from hierarchical control and presidential removal. Americans expect judge-like independence when politicians grant administrators judge-like powers and functions.

The quasi-judicial category deployed in Humphrey's was the logical extension of English legal customs, Founding Era administration, and the evolution of the ninteenth-century law of officeholding. It reflected an Anglo-American instinct to insulate judge-like offices from direct hierarchical control. Whether you are an originalist or a believer in the history-and-tradition approach, these findings show that Congress may insulate quasi-judicial officials from presidential removal and direction. Beyond original public meaning, the quasi-judicial function from Humphrey's is bound up with the Anglo-American constitutional project stretching back beyond the Founding. If the Roberts Court overrules Humphrey's, it will imperil a primordial instinct that is part of our rule-of-law tradition.

detail.title: Payment Choice and the Pain of Paying: Evidence on Tipping Behavior from Payment Diary Data
detail.abstract: We examine how payment methods and the perceived pain of paying shape tipping behavior. Using unique transaction-level payment diary data from Switzerland for 2024-2025, we estimate the effects of the most common payment instruments—cash, debit and credit cards, and mobile payments—on both the likelihood and amount of tipping. We also analyze how subjective pain of paying interacts with these tipping choices. Our results show that both payment method and the pain of paying exert statistically and economically significant influences on tipping behavior. Relative to cash, electronic payment methods are associated with a lower probability of tipping. However, this difference in tipping probability between the payment methods disappears when the bill totals a round amount, i.e. a multiple of CHF 5 or CHF 10. Conditional on tipping, electronic payment methods result in smaller tip amounts for an average bill amount of CHF 32.45. However, this effect reverts for bill amounts larger than CHF 90. We find no meaningful difference in tipping behavior between contactless and chip-and-PIN card transactions.

title: Pillar Two Side-by-Side Challenges of EU Law, Global Tax Governance, Sovereignty. Comments for a Rational Win-Win Path Forward

detail.abstract: The European Union has transposed Pillar Two into EU law, requiring Member States to implement a top-up tax system, including an income-inclusion rule (IIR) and an undertaxed profits rule (UTPR), to ensure that every in-scope MNE pays an effective rate of at least 15 percent in each jurisdiction starting 2026.[1] Republicans of the Ways and Means Committee, from whence tax legislation originates, have this week (the first week of December 2025) stated that if a Pillar Two Side-by-Side agreement (the “Agreement”)[2] with the U.S. Treasury is not in place by year’s end, then Congress will re-propose the retaliatory I.R.C. Section 899.[3] Meanwhile, I.R.C. Section 891, enacted in 1934, remains as an active retaliation standby, albeit nearly all EU countries have a tax treaty with the U.S. that is “last in time.” The U.S. minimum tax regime and the Pillar 2 regime are certainly not identical; otherwise, there would not be a need to hammer out a comparability agreement. But neither does the U.S. minimum corporate tax regime establish a more tax-competitive environment for U.S. headquartered multinationals. The U.S. minimum corporate tax regime is comprised of four core elements: (1) controlled foreign corporation deemed income inclusion pursuant to Subpart F, (2) controlled foreign corporation deemed income inclusion pursuant to Net CFC Tested Income (NCTI) (formerly GILTI before 2026), (3) the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax (CAMT), and (4) the Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT). The NCTI aspect of the U.S. minimum corporate tax regime does not allow either of the significant Pillar 2 exclusions: the substance-based income exclusion or the qualified refundable tax credit exception.[4] When the four aspects are examined in totality, we find a robust tax web with significantly higher compliance costs than any EU regime under Pillar 2; indeed, not a lenient leaky bucket.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a decadal review of India–U.S. trade relations from 2012 to 2022, focusing on trends in exports, imports, and trade balance. Using official government data and a quantitative framework, the analysis divides the period into pre-COVID (2012–2019) and post-COVID (2019–2022) phases to capture both long-term structural dynamics and the impact of global disruption. Results show that India consistently maintained a trade surplus, driven by labor-intensive and resourcebased exports such as textiles and pharmaceuticals, while the U.S. dominated in capital- and technology-intensive goods. The COVID-19 shock temporarily reduced trade volumes in 2020, but recovery was rapid, with 2021–2022 reflecting renewed momentum and diversification. The study concludes that bilateral trade is structurally resilient and strategically significant, supported by complementary advantages and reinforced by global supply-chain shifts. These findings underline the importance of the India–U.S. partnership as a stabilizing force in global economic relations.

title: Testing Parametric Distribution Family Assumptions via Differences in Differential Entropy
affiliations: Washington State University, University of California, Berkeley - Department of Agricultural & Resource Economics and OnPoint Analytics, Inc.

detail.title: Testing Parametric Distribution Family Assumptions via Differences in Differential Entropy
detail.abstract: We present a widely applicable statistical testing procedure for assessing the validity of hypotheses that postulate which family of parametric distributions generated a random sample of data. The test provides a unified framework for testing across a wide scope of distribution families, and has asymptotic validity derived directly from established maximum likelihood, bootstrapping, and kernel density estimator (KDE) principles. It is straightforward to implement, interpret, and can be efficiently calculated. Moreover, the test is constructive in the sense of being informative regardless of whether the null hypothesis is rejected or not, where in the latter case, the outcome suggests that the hypothesized distribution can be close to the actual distribution of the data. The test is based on the concept of differential entropy and the degree of divergence between two different sample estimates of differential entropy, one being a direct MLE estimate under the null hypothesis and the other being a nonparametric estimate derived from a bootstrapped KDE calculation of differential entropy. We refer to the testing principal as the Difference in Differential Entropy (DDE) approach for testing hypotheses about parametric families of distributions. Choosing the values of tuning parameters, evaluation points, or grids is automated and thus not required, nor is there a concern about complicated idiosyncratic regularity conditions. The test is implemented by choosing a parametric family of distributions as the null distribution from a large catalogue of possible families, and the test then proceeds by following a consistent and well-defined procedure from that point forward. Sampling experiments illustrate the application of the test and its finite sample behavior, including its notable size accuracy and empirical power even for relatively small samples of data. Three sets of data from the historical literature form the basis for three empirical applications of the procedure that provide additional insights about research outcomes relative to them.

title: Curvature-Calibrated Wald Confidence Ellipsoids in Nonlinear Regression
affiliations: Rajamangala University of Technology Suvarnabhumi, Heriot-Watt University and Rajamangala University of Technology Suvarnabhumi

detail.title: Curvature-Calibrated Wald Confidence Ellipsoids in Nonlinear Regression
detail.abstract: Wald-type confidence ellipsoids are widely used for inference in nonlinear regression owing to their simple closed form, but their finite-sample coverage can deteriorate severely in the presence of model curvature. This paper develops a curvature-calibrated Wald ellipsoid that preserves the usual analytic form while explicitly accounting for nonlinearity. Building on intrinsic and parameter-effects curvature in the sense of Bates and Watts, together with a higher-order expansion of the nonlinear least squares estimator, we introduce a curvature factor κ(θ 0) that controls the nonlinear remainder and yields an explicit, data-dependent upper bound on the coverage error of the standard Wald region. This bound motivates a simple inflation of the conventional χ 2 cutoff and leads to a corrected ellipsoid C * 1-α that attains (or slightly exceeds) the nominal coverage within an appropriate linearization region, while requiring only quantities available from standard nonlinear regression software. A simulation study based on Michaelis-Menten, exponential decay, and logistic growth models compares classical Wald, curvature-calibrated, and likelihood-ratio regions. In moderately nonlinear settings, the calibrated ellipsoid substantially improves coverage relative to Wald and typically matches or outperforms likelihood-ratio regions with only modest volume inflation. In more severely curved, weakly identifiable scenarios, it still improves coverage but does not fully restore the nominal level, thereby delineating the practical limits of this simple curvature-based correction.

detail.title:
Ecological Economics
Public Spending, Labor Markets, and Ecological Transition in a Coastal Regional Economy
detail.abstract: This study examines how regional public spending contributes to sustainable and inclusive employment outcomes in North Sulawesi, Indonesia-a coastal socioecological region where livelihoods depend on fisheries, tourism, agriculture, and natural resource stewardship. Moving beyond conventional fiscal analyses, employment is positioned as a socio-ecological pathway linking public finance, human well-being, and regional sustainability. Using a panel dataset from 15 districts and cities for 2020-2024, we apply Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA) on regional fiscal, labour, demographic, and skill-development indicators to evaluate both direct and conditional effects of public spending on employment. Results show that public expenditure has a statistically significant positive impact on labour absorption, confirming its role as a key instrument for inclusive development. However, macroeconomic conditions, demographic structure, and skill development programs do not significantly strengthen this relationship, indicating limited policy integration for a just and ecologically aligned employment transition. The findings reveal that while fiscal policy stimulates jobs, synergy with green-skills programs, ecological investment priorities, and place-based development strategies remains weak. Strengthening ecological public finance, enhancing community-based labour capacity-including local cooperative traditions such as Mapalus-and directing spending toward green and resilience-oriented sectors are essential to support sustainable employment growth. This study contributes to ecological economics by framing public spending as a tool for socio-ecological resilience and highlighting the need for integrated, place-based fiscal policies in Indonesia's regional economies.

title: Optimal Auction Design under Costly Learning
affiliations: University of Southampton

detail.title: Optimal Auction Design under Costly Learning
detail.abstract: We study optimal auction design in an independent private values environment where bidders can endogenously-but at a cost-improve information about their own valuations. The optimal mechanism is two-stage: at stage-1 bidders register an information acquisition plan and pay a transfer; at stage-2 they bid, and allocation and payments are determined. We show that the revenue-optimal stage-2 rule is the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) mechanism, while stage-1 transfers implement the optimal screening of types and absorb information rents consistent with incentive compatibility and participation. By committing to VCG ex post, the pre-auction information game becomes a potential game, so equilibrium information choices maximize expected welfare; the stage-1 fee schedule then transfers an optimal amount of payoff without conditioning on unverifiable cost scales. The design is robust to asymmetric primitives and accommodates a wide range of information technologies, providing a simple implementation that unifies efficiency and optimal revenue in environments with endogenous information acquisition.

title: Too Slow for the AI Age? An Overview of the Dynamic Research Continuum

detail.title: Too Slow for the AI Age? An Overview of the Dynamic Research Continuum
detail.abstract: Contemporary artificial intelligence evolves on a quarterly cycle while academic publishing often runs on much longer timeframes. That tempo mismatch creates what this paper calls an AI impact gap: a growing space where AI systems reshape economies and institutions faster than independent evidence can be produced, vetted, and synthesized. In that space, epistemic authority flows to corporate labs, vendors, and informal commentary rather than to public, peer reviewed knowledge (Naddaf, 2024; Suber, 2012). This companion piece summarizes the argument of "Too Slow for the AI Age? Building a Dynamic Research Continuum." (Simpson, 2025a). It reconstructs how legacy constraints in journal publishing produced slow and opaque evidence pipelines (Garfield, 2006; Powell, 2016; Vale, 2015), reviews partial reforms such as preprints, open peer review, and living systematic reviews and then outlines a proposed Dynamic Research Continuum (DRC). DRC is a versioned, openly reviewed, and continuously synthesized publication architecture explicitly designed for highvelocity AI domains. The paper also introduces the Iterative Human-AI Co-Creation (IHACC) framework as the workflow layer that lets human experts and AI systems collaborate without collapsing into naive automation (Simpson, 2025b). Together, DRC and IHACC aim to restore temporal legitimacy to evidence-informed governance in the AI age by shortening the distance between new results, credible synthesis, and real-world decisions.

detail.abstract:
Nature degradation is increasingly recognised as a systemic source of economic and financial risk, yet the mechanisms linking private financial flows to global biodiversity loss remain insufficiently understood. For the United Kingdom, potential GDP losses of up to 12% by the 2030s highlight the macroeconomic significance of ecosystem decline. Given that roughly half of the UK’s nature-related financial risk is generated outside its borders, analysing the international biodiversity impacts of UK-financed activities is essential for informing governance strategies aligned with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF). This study integrates financial exposure data, ecosystem-service dependency assessments and environmental-pressure modelling to evaluate how UK banks’ overseas portfolios both depend on and contribute to ecological degradation.

We map cross-border exposures for the six largest UK banks, quantify sectoral dependencies and risks using the ENCORE framework, and assess portfolio impacts across thirteen categories of environmental pressure. While financial flows are concentrated in manufacturing and services, we find that high-impact sectors—agriculture, mining and transport—generate disproportionate pressures through land conversion, pollution, and resource extraction. Risks are most pronounced for ecosystem services related to flood protection, water regulation and climate regulation. Exploratory scenario analysis, combining nature-action pathways with geopolitical dynamics, demonstrates that coordinated policy interventions—particularly subsidy reforms and a global plastics treaty—could generate meaningful reductions in nutrient pollution, biotic resource extraction and solid-waste generation. A complementary assessment of green financial regulation indicates that mandatory disclosures, capital and collateral adjustments, and allocative credit policies could reduce financing linked to land-use change, though their effectiveness depends on international cooperation to prevent financial leakage.

Overall, the findings underscore the interdependence of financial systems and ecological integrity, and illustrate how coherent regulatory, fiscal and trade measures could realign UK financial flows with global biodiversity goals. The study highlights the need for integrated governance approaches capable of addressing cross-border ecological risks embedded within contemporary financial globalisation.

title: Soaked Orders, Shifted Liquidity: Extreme Precipitation and Trade Credit in Global Supply Chains
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Business, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Economics & Finance, City University of Hong Kong and Xiamen University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Soaked Orders, Shifted Liquidity: Extreme Precipitation and Trade Credit in Global Supply Chains
detail.abstract: Climate change has been increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation, yet how these shocks transmit through global supply chains remains unclear. This study documents the downstream-to-upstream transmission of climate risk. Leveraging a global panel of firm-level supply chain links, we show that extreme precipitation at customers' locations reduces suppliers' accounts receivable, indicating a demand-driven contraction in trade credit. The contraction is attenuated for suppliers with weaker bargaining power, shorter customer relationship tenure, and lower leverage. Our evidence indicates that suppliers are absorbing customers' liquidity shocks. These findings highlight a demand-side pathway for the transmission of climate shocks in supply chains, delineate the conditions under which trade credit shifts liquidity shocks, and offer a network perspective guidance for firms and regulators seeking to strengthen global production supply chains.

title: Expected Liquidation Values
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System,  and McGill University

detail.title: Expected Liquidation Values
detail.abstract: We use supervisory commercial real estate data to create the first forward-looking measure of expected liquidation values in default. Loans secured by collateral with higher liquidation values, relative to their current market values, are larger, have longer maturities and are less likely to be renegotiated. In the time series, there is a strong relationship between industry-level stock returns and changes in liquidation values, even after controlling for contemporaneous changes in current property values. Finally, the pass-through of industry shocks is amplified among property types with more correlated default rates. Our results provide support for incomplete contracting theory and industry-driven fire sales. Finally, our new measure of expected liquidation costs can be used by policymakers to monitor fire sale risk in real time.

title: The Value of Government Debt with Domestic Arrears

detail.title: The Value of Government Debt with Domestic Arrears
detail.abstract: This paper documents the use of domestic arrears, i.e. overdue payments by the government to its domestic beneficiaries, as a form of alternative financing used to improve the valuation of government bonds and, thus, satisfy public financing needs. For my analysis, I use a historical dataset from the UK (1700-1900), where Army and Navy Bills served as payment to merchants when cash payments were delayed. I find that arrears, whose face value averages 4.3 percent of GDP, have a risk-adjusted present value of 12.9 percent of GDP on average. By creating arrears, the government increases fiscal space, allowing the issuance of more bonds, compared to a no-arrears counterfactual. The intuition is that arrears accumulate during bad times and redirect cash flows from suppliers to bondholders: thus, they provide risk-averse bondholders with an insurance-like cash flow that justifies higher bond valuations. The omission of arrears in the valuation of public marketable debt leads to an underestimation of its fundamental value either through mismeasurement of government expenditures, or due to the disregard of revenues extracted from suppliers via financial repression. The paper contributes to the resolution of recently raised public debt valuation puzzles and provides a new rationale for the emergence of arrears. Finally, an estimated dataset of payment arrears for EU member countries is presented, revealing size and cyclicality akin to the historical UK data.

title: The Impact of the OBBBA on the South Korean Battery Sector

detail.title: The Impact of the OBBBA on the South Korean Battery Sector

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 25/MER/07/01
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The South Korean battery industry is navigating a period of significant difficulty. Corporate performance has deteriorated sharply in the wake of the so-called “EV chasm,” a period in which the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) has slowed. Global market share is trending downward, and the United States has rolled back policies that support EV adoption even as Korean firms pursue massive investments in EV and battery production stateside. These three factors are causally interlinked.

First, even as overall EV demand has contracted, relative demand for cost-effective, mid-to-low-range EVs has expanded. This phenomenon has meant that Chinese-made lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batterymakers have gained market share, while demand for Korea's ternary batteries has declined. Second, the EV chasm has been most severe in Europe, where EV and battery sales plummeted in countries that rolled back their subsidy programs, with the drop occurring immediately after the policy changes took effect. EVs are still more expensive than their internal combustion engine (ICE) counterparts, and government subsidies have been essential to bridging the price gap; the elimination or reduction of these subsidies in many countries has had a direct impact on battery demand. Third, the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) in the US brought an end to the EV purchase tax credit. This too will inevitably have a negative impact on the Korean battery industry. In Europe, EV sales fell by 27 percent in Germany and three percent in France after those countries rolled back their EV subsidies; the US market is highly likely to follow a similar path. Furthermore, even the Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit (AMPC) — which remains in effect — will be negatively affected, because if declining sales lead Korean firms to cut production in the US, the value of their AMPC benefits will decline in sync. However, the OBBBA also made it much more difficult for Chinese firms to enter US supply chains and benefit from the AMPC, meaning a European-style loss of market share to China is unlikely.

To overcome this confluence of challenges and build on past successes, what measures should the Korean battery industry take? The most urgent task is undoubtedly to stimulate a recovery in the EV market by enhancing battery performance and lowering costs through technological and process innovation. This paper, however, proposes a complementary strategy: to proactively create and capture new sources of demand beyond the EV sector. Military drones and humanoid robots are prime examples. These emerging sectors share three key characteristics: they are poised to evolve into massive markets, are central arenas in the US-China technology rivalry, and, most importantly, they require high-performance batteries. Thus, they hold immense market potential for Korean companies.

detail.title: Human Edge, Machine Limits: AI-Human Competition in Financial Markets
detail.abstract: We develop a theoretical framework to study competition between AI-powered and human investors with heterogeneous sophistication. Human investors possess superior private information but are limited by bounded strategic reasoning, modeled through a cognitive-hierarchy structure. AI investors, in contrast, learn and trade through reinforcement learning that autonomously optimizes trading profits over time. We show that human investors can consistently outperform sophisticated AI investors because AI sophistication is constrained by the data it learns from, which reflects the behavior of the average rather than the most advanced human trader. Three forces limit AI profitability: (i) the advantage of human private information, (ii) the price-stabilizing actions of the most sophisticated human traders, and (iii) the growing price impact of AI trading as its market share expands. Together, these mechanisms reveal the limits of algorithmic superiority and provide a foundation for understanding AI–human competition in financial markets.

It is worth noting, though, that since the enactment of the Refugee Act, the yearly number of asylum seekers has increased nearly tenfold, surpassing 18,000 in 2023. title: Remaking the State from Below: Local Government Formation in Ukraine
affiliations: Einaudi Institute for Economics and Finance (EIEF)

detail.title: Remaking the State from Below: Local Government Formation in Ukraine
detail.abstract: Does consolidating local governments while expanding their autonomy improve governance and development? I study Ukraine's 2015-2020 reform, which allowed small local councils to voluntarily amalgamate into newly created hromadas with greater fiscal and administrative authority. Councils that were wealthier, more Ukrainian-speaking and more similar to their neighbors were more likely to merge. Exploiting the staggered rollout of the reform, I show that amalgamation improved procurement performance, increased local economic activity, and strengthened civic national identity. The share of highly competitive tenders and the average number of bidders per tender rose, and local public expenditures expanded and shifted toward social sectors. Nightlights per capita increased by about 7%, consistent with higher economic activity. Survey evidence further shows that residents of rural areas, who were most exposed to the reform, were more likely to identify solely as Ukrainian. The gains were particularly pronounced for smaller hromadas and for peripheral local councils within merged units. These findings suggest that consolidating jurisdictions while devolving authority can enhance state effectiveness, stimulate local development and shape civic identity.

title: The Nobel Prize in Economics and the Predicament of Mainstream Economics: The Degeneration from Institutional Determinism to Cultural Determinism
affiliations: Independent researcher

detail.title: The Nobel Prize in Economics and the Predicament of Mainstream Economics: The Degeneration from Institutional Determinism to Cultural Determinism
detail.abstract: This paper critically examines how the Nobel Prizes in Economic Sciences from 2024 to 2025 reveal a regression within mainstream economic theory. The 2024 award reaffirmed the importance of institutions in shaping economic prosperity, whereas the 2025 award shifted the explanatory framework from institutional determinism to cultural determinism. This shift represents not theoretical progress but intellectual regression—an evasion of institutional complexity through the abstract narrative of “culture.” The paper argues that mainstream economics remains trapped in the illusion of market self-correction, externalizing structural deficiencies as “externalities” while neglecting the institutional mechanisms that sustain macroeconomic stability. Cultural determinism further distorts the understanding of institutional transformation, allowing non-democratic regimes to justify policy failure under the pretext of “cultural backwardness.” Building on recent theoretical developments (Huang 2025a, 2025b, 2025c) and related institutional research (Stiglitz 2010; North 1990), the paper contends that macroeconomic theory must shift from a wealth-creation paradigm centered on market efficiency to a wealth-distribution paradigm grounded in fiscal coordination and institutional design. The reconstruction of macroeconomics, therefore, must rest on institutional realism rather than cultural idealism.

title: 위성자료를 활용한 북한 소비시장 변화와 무역에 관한 연구(A Study of North Korean Consumer Market Changes and Trade Using Satellite Data)

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: As North Korea continues to blockade its borders, it is difficult to study the North Korean economy. The purpose of this study is to analyze North Korea’s market activities by using satellite data in a new way and to identify the characteristics of market development over time. This study is different from previous studies in that it is the first to attempt a quantitative analysis of North Korea’s mar- kets and logistics using satellite data. To complement the analysis of the market and logistics, this study also analyzes the changes in import, wholesale, and retail prices in North Korea, which is also different from previous studies in that it analyzes wholesale and retail margins for the first time to identify the role of wholesale and retail merchants.(The rest omitted.)

title: The Long-Run Effects of Tropical Cyclones on the U.S. Housing Market

detail.title: The Long-Run Effects of Tropical Cyclones on the U.S. Housing Market
detail.abstract: Housing is a major component of wealth in the United States. Despite tropical cyclones causing approximately $1.3 trillion in damages since 1980, there is limited empirical evidence on their long-term effects on the housing market. This paper examines the impact of tropical cyclones on housing values in the contiguous U.S. from 1988 to 2021. Using data from the National Hurricane Center and a radial wind-speed model, I construct a new cyclone exposure measure and provide the first plausibly causal estimates of the aggregate impact of all recorded cyclones at the county-year level. Despite a shortterm rise, housing values decline by 15% over an eight-year horizon following cyclone exposure. Within coastal counties, areas with lower historical cyclone activity tend to have more housing development and higher property values, suggesting households sort into seemingly safer locations. However, these less-experienced areas suffer the most persistent declines. One key mechanism of decreasing housing prices appears to be a sharp increase in insurance uptake, contributing to higher post-disaster living costs. These findings highlight that cyclone risk is driven not just by exposure but also by local preparedness.

title: Awkward Silence: Is Manager Hesitation Informative?

detail.title: Awkward Silence: Is Manager Hesitation Informative?
detail.abstract: I study whether managers' hesitation conveys information about future firm performance as well as analysts' behavior. Hesitation is defined as the response time (RT) between analyst questions and managerial answers, measured using AI-based speaker diarization and transcript alignment over 7,000 earnings calls from S&P 500 firms (2019-2023). I find that longer RT is associated with lower contemporaneous and 1-quarter ahead cumulative abnormal returns. Analysts revise earnings forecasts downward and demonstrate increased uncertainty, through higher forecast dispersion. RT fails to predict future earning surprises, a finding consistent with analysts promptly and efficiently incorporating the hesitation signal into their forecasts. This paper is among the first to show that silence, specifically managerial response time, can serve as an additional, non-verbal information channel. The findings contribute to the literature on information asymmetry, behavioral finance, and provide empirical support for the information uncertainty explanation of post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD).

title: Growth of Income Funds and Death of Volatility: A Study of Inelastic Option Supply and Market Impact
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas and

detail.title: Growth of Income Funds and Death of Volatility: A Study of Inelastic Option Supply and Market Impact
detail.abstract: Over the past decade, income funds employing the call overwriting strategy have emerged as one of the fastest-growing segments in the mutual fund industry. This study explores the consequential impact of these income funds on the underlying assets and options. By using detailed option positions of all mutual funds from N-PORT disclosure, notably, the aggregate selling of call options by these income funds reduces subsequent monthly option implied / realized volatility and option returns. Its predictive power stems from income funds, which repetitively overwrite calls rather than engaging in informed selling for volatility timing, indicating that the inelastic supply from repetitively selling in option markets from these funds influences volatility, and their impact does not stem from volatility timing but from their sizable selling pressure. In the context of demand based asset pricing, this is an important implication because such a repeated inelastic demand of overwriting can detrimentally impact potential profits, as lower implied volatility diminishes the option premium, and consequently reduce the cash flow stream for investors of income funds.

title: Rationalizable Behavior in Matching with Externalities *
affiliations: University of Padua - Department of Economics and Management,  and University of Padua - Department of Economics

detail.title: Rationalizable Behavior in Matching with Externalities *
detail.abstract: In many matching problems, it is natural to assume that agents may have preferences not only over their own potential partners but also over the matches formed by others. Once such externalities are taken into account, the set of stable matchings depends on what agents believe would occur if they were to deviate. We introduce a notion of preference-dependent beliefs, called rationalizable conjectures which parallels the notion of rationalizability in non-cooperative games. We define the set of Rationalizable Conjecturally Stable matchings and show that it is always non empty. We also introduce the notion of rationalizability for matching and prove that every rationalizable conjecturally stable matching is indeed rationalizable. We show that rationalizability for matching is behaviorally implied by the epistemic condition of pairwise rationality and common belief in pairwise rationality, whereas rationalizable conjectural stability additionally requires belief correctness. Unlike our approach, traditional pairwise stability in matching with externalities depends on strong and implausible epistemic conditions.

title: A Peace Positive Enterprise for the Global South: Problem Statements, Alternative Perspectives, and Paths Forward
affiliations: Stellenbosch Business School

detail.title: A Peace Positive Enterprise for the Global South: Problem Statements, Alternative Perspectives, and Paths Forward

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was secured.
declarations.funderStatement: Funding was provided in part by the Research Council of Norway under the grant, Peace Positive Private Sector Development in Africa (P3A)

detail.abstract: Contemporary European and broader international policy posit within the liberal tradition the peacebuilding and development potential of the profit seeking corporation, with attendant focus on incorporating MNC perspectives and needs into development narratives and strategies. However, conflict affected places across the Global South are distinct across multiple dimensions, creating dilemmas for the establishment and sustainability of ethical corporations that contribute to peaceful and inclusive development but all the same must accommodate Northern financial, strategic, and operational logics. This conceptual paper explores these tensions, drawing on interviews and convenings with diverse thought leaders across sectors concerned with business, human security, and peaceful development in conflict contexts informed by insights from the political economy of conflict. Deliberations expose divergent understandings between Northern advocates and Southern critics of how large enterprises may need to differ across more and less peaceful places. By shifting policy deliberation and research towards the problem statements that emerge, we may better incorporate Global South perspectives to imagine the distinctive contours of future business at scale that is more reliably able to advance peaceful and inclusive development in contexts of acute socio-political contestation. Such inquiry would help to decolonize scholarship as it adds nuance to policy debates.

title: How Politics Shapes the Environmental Impact of Large Infrastructure Projects: Evidence from Road Construction in Brazil
affiliations: FGV/Brazil,  and FGV-SP

detail.title: How Politics Shapes the Environmental Impact of Large Infrastructure Projects: Evidence from Road Construction in Brazil
detail.abstract: Existing work argues that road expansion unavoidably leads to forest loss. We maintain instead that this relationship is conditional on policy choices. Specifically, command-and-control and market-based policies can reshape land-use incentives to prevent new clearing, especially when they operate together through policy coordination. We study a 2005 programme created to minimise environmental degradation while a major highway was paved across Brazil's Cerrado and Amazon. We use a staggered difference-indifferences design and a unique dataset to estimate the effect of the Programme on deforestation and how this effect varied depending on the deployment of enforcement and conditional credit. We find substantial reductions in forest loss; these effects concentrate where enforcement and conditional credit rise together, and the revocation of the Programme erases conservation gains. The results show that the environmental footprint of roads is a policy choice, contingent on whether states employ the right policy instruments to induce sustainable land-use.

title: Markets: Traditional Perception and Modern Behaviour
affiliations: Srinivas University and Poornaprajna College in Udupi.

detail.title: Markets: Traditional Perception and Modern Behaviour

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No financial elationship involved
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethical conflicts
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding

detail.abstract: This paper explores the evolving nature of markets by juxtaposing traditional perceptions with contemporary behavioural dynamics. Historically, markets have been perceived as structured spaces governed by rational decision-making and classical economic principles. However, the advent of digital technologies, globalization, and insights from behavioural economics has reshaped market behaviour, challenging foundational assumptions. Drawing on interdisciplinary frameworks, the paper examines how consumer psychology, information asymmetry, and technological platforms influence modern market outcomes. Case studies from both physical and digital marketplaces illustrate the divergence from traditional models, highlighting the complexity and adaptability of current economic interactions. By critically analysing these shifts, the paper offers a nuanced understanding of market transformation and its implications for policy, regulation, and economic theory.

title: Environmental, Energy Security, and Equity (3E) Implications of Decarbonization Pathways in Nepal: An Open-Source OSeMOSYS Analysis
affiliations: Tribhuvan University

detail.title: Environmental, Energy Security, and Equity (3E) Implications of Decarbonization Pathways in Nepal: An Open-Source OSeMOSYS Analysis
detail.abstract: Low-and middle-income countries must expand modern energy access while aligning with netzero pledges. We developed an open, least-cost OSeMOSYS model of Nepal's power sector calibrated to 2022-2024 statistics and policy targets to assess three pathways to 2050: Business-as-Usual (BAU), Accelerated Electrification with RDF utilization (REW-Diversification), and Net-Zero Emissions (NZE). Hydropower was parameterized with Nepal-specific seasonal availability reflecting monsoon and dry-season flows. Outcomes were evaluated on environmental (direct CO₂), energy-security (import dependence, resource diversity, adequacy margin), and equity proxies (household electricity burden; electrified shares of cooking, transport, and industrial heat). BAU produced rising emissions (≈13.8 Mt in 2022 to ≈24.5 Mt by 2050) and growing dry-season import exposure. REW reduced 2050 emissions to ≈7 Mt at the lowest discounted system cost (≈US$83.1 bn), driven by end-use electrification (e-cooking; e-buses/two-wheelers), rapid solar build-out with storage, and RDF/modern bioenergy for high-temperature industrial heat. NZE achieved near-zero power-sector emissions by 2050 with only a modest cost premium (≈US$83.8 bn) and improved security and equity indicators relative to BAU, including lower import dependence and higher adequacy in dry seasons. Cross-border power trade acted as a cost-and risk-hedge when priced within observed ranges. Sensitivity analysis identified hydropower availability and storage costs as first-order drivers; results were robust to discount-rate and import-price variations. The open workflow provides a transparent, reproducible template for hydropower-reliant LMICs to co-optimize climate, security, and affordability under hydro-climate uncertainty.

title: Is Globalization Ending? Evidence and Policy Evaluation
affiliations: Universiti Kuala Lumpur Business School and Westminster International University in Tashkent (WIUT)

detail.title: Is Globalization Ending? Evidence and Policy Evaluation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NONE
declarations.ethicsApproval: NONE
declarations.funderStatement: NONE

detail.abstract:
This paper aims to provide an in-depth evaluation of the decline of globalization. Hence, we suggest a Deglobalization Index (Ð-Index) that utilizes economic and security indicators to track the shift from integration to fragmentation (1990–2025). The proposed model is key findings show peak globalization in 1996–
2000, a post-2008 break, and a sharp rise in deglobalization after 2021. Policy evaluation suggests the need for new national economic strategies that emphasize friend-shoring and regional diversification, interoperable standards and transparent export controls, targeted buffers for critical goods, and WTO compatible plurilateral to manage protectionist pressures. These measures reduce exposure to shocks while preserving efficiency. We conclude with a prioritized policy agenda balancing resilience and openness.

title:
Safe-Haven Currency and Sequence Risk
A State-Dependent Swiss Franc Overlay for Global Portfolios

detail.title:
Safe-Haven Currency and Sequence Risk
A State-Dependent Swiss Franc Overlay for Global Portfolios
detail.abstract: Sequence-of-returns risk (SoRR) arises because the order of returns-not only their long-run average-determines whether real, inflation-indexed spending plans survive the first critical withdrawal years. For households that spend in EUR or JPY yet invest in globally diversified, USD-centric portfolios, SoRR is co-determined by market and FX paths in the spending currency. We evaluate SoRR explicitly in the spending currency and present a small, state-dependent overlay in Swiss franc cash/bills (CHF) as crisis insurance, not generic hedging. Motivated by documented safe-haven behavior of CHF and evidence that global bonds are best held fully hedged into the home currency, we specify a transparent trigger rule based on a composite stress score and assess sequence-sensitive objectives (CVaR(95), maximum drawdowns, time-underwater, and the 5th percentile of sustainable withdrawals) alongside real-terms withdrawal recursions. FX and index procedures follow the WM/Refinitiv 4pm Fix and MSCI index methodology. The design is complete and replicable; empirical tables/figures can be added modularly without altering methods.

title: Landslide Susceptibility Evaluation of Chenab River Valley Locations in Jammu & Kashmir Based On Analytic Hierarchy Process Using Geospatial Technique
affiliations: Central University of Karnataka and Government College Attingal

detail.title: Landslide Susceptibility Evaluation of Chenab River Valley Locations in Jammu & Kashmir Based On Analytic Hierarchy Process Using Geospatial Technique

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest related to the publication of this paper

detail.abstract: Landslides in the Chenab River Valley endanger human and animal lives, agricultural lands, infrastructure, and the socioeconomic stability of rural communities. This study focuses on landslide susceptibility mapping of the Chenab River Valley using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) integrated with Remote Sensing (RS) and Geographic Information System (GIS) techniques. A comprehensive geospatial database of conditioning factors was created, and susceptibility zones were defined to identify areas with varying vulnerability. The AHP-based model had an AUC accuracy of 83%, indicating excellent predictive performance. The study found that 18.7796 km² falls under highly vulnerable zones, accounting for 0.04% of the total landslide area, while 70% occurred in the moderate susceptibility zone. High-risk zones were concentrated along steeper slopes and near roads, emphasising the impact of topography and human activities. The resulting susceptibility map is an important tool for planners, engineers, and decision-makers to implement preventive and mitigation measures, thereby promoting sustainable development and hazard management in the Chenab River Valley.

title: Current State and Analysis of Regulatory Requirements for Energy Efficiency of Buildings
affiliations: Institute of General Energy of NAS of Ukraine

detail.title: Current State and Analysis of Regulatory Requirements for Energy Efficiency of Buildings
detail.abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive analysis of energy efficiency in buildings, focusing on regulatory requirements, current practices, and the state of energy efficiency in Ukraine and worldwide. It examines the substantial energy consumption in the construction sector and the inefficiencies in Ukraine's housing stock, emphasizing the need for thermal modernization and reduced energy consumption in residential buildings. The impact of European Union energy efficiency standards on construction projects is explored, along with measures implemented in Ukraine for improvement. Key considerations such as the interaction of building elements, air exchange, and development of a mathematical model for thermal conditions and heat losses are highlighted. The significance of optimizing indoor air quality and managing air exchange rates to balance energy savings and occupant comfort is discussed, alongside standards and regulations from the US and the EU. The paper delves into ventilation rates, air exchange requirements, CO2 level measurement, and the use of natural and mechanical ventilation systems. It extends the analysis to estimating infiltration in commercial buildings using various coefficients and considers the importance of hourly climate data and software tools for accurate energy performance assessments. Additionally, the research addresses the health impacts of indoor air pollutants, such as carbon dioxide, bioeffluents, and particulate matter, and underscores the importance of compliance with WHO guidelines and national standards for maintaining healthy indoor environments. Empirical studies on natural ventilation, adaptive comfort, and the effect of pollutants on cognitive performance are reviewed. The paper also incorporates a broad range of sources, offering valuable insights into the optimization of indoor environmental quality and energy efficiency in buildings, with specific focus on thermal comfort, the role of occupant behavior, and methodologies for indoor climate monitoring and energy performance assessment.

title: Learning to Fly: How Canadians Can Navigate a More Complex Financial Landscape
affiliations: HEC Montreal and Independent

detail.title: Learning to Fly: How Canadians Can Navigate a More Complex Financial Landscape
detail.abstract:
• Canadians are managing more money and more financial decisions than ever. Over the past 30 years, household wealth has more than doubled, while traditional supports like workplace pensions have faded. With fewer defined benefit plans and limited growth in public retirement benefits, people have to make more choices on their own – about saving, investing, and when to retire.

  • Most people aren’t fully prepared for those choices. Financial literacy in Canada remains low, and many struggle with basic concepts like compound interest, inflation, investment risk, and taxes. These gaps can lead to costly mistakes – choosing the wrong savings plan, paying high fees, or missing out on investment returns – especially as retirement decisions become more complex.

  • Technology can help, but financial literacy remains the foundation. Artificial intelligence could make financial learning and advice more accessible and affordable. Still, people need a basic level of understanding to use it safely. Governments and regulators should set clear leadership and guardrails for AI in personal finance, support quality advice, and make financial education a bigger part of helping Canadians chart their course and reach financial security safely.

title: BPHM: A Large Language Model-Enabled Bio-Inspired Prognostics and Health Management Framework for Autonomous Reliability Assurance in Cloud-Edge Systems
affiliations: Southwest Jiaotong University, Southwest Jiaotong University, Southwest Jiaotong University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Southwest Jiaotong University

detail.title: BPHM: A Large Language Model-Enabled Bio-Inspired Prognostics and Health Management Framework for Autonomous Reliability Assurance in Cloud-Edge Systems
detail.abstract: With the increasing application of artificial intelligence, cloud-edge collaboration necessitates deep integration to meet the demands of AI applications, including model training, deployment, and data collection. However, this integrated and collaborative system architecture also introduces unprecedented complexity, posing significant challenges for fault diagnosis, remediation, and reliability assurance in cloud-edge systems. This paper proposes a Bio-Inspired Prognostics and Health Management Framework (BPHM) framework for ensuring autonomous reliability of cloud-edge systems. By mimicking the sensing, diagnostic, restorative, and learning mechanisms of biological nervous systems, it achieves comprehensive and intelligent fault management for edge device clusters. In response to potential system failures, this paper proposes a method based on large models for autonomous fault learning and autonomous reliability assurance, which can effectively prevent certain types of failures. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework exhibits excellent performance in zero-shot fault diagnosis tasks, achieving an average diagnostic accuracy of 88.75%, while also meeting the requirements for low-latency inference. This research provides a novel approach for autonomous reliability assurance and intelligent fault tolerance in cloud-edge collaborative systems.

title: The Sovereign Dilemma: A Critical Analysis of Startup Re-Domiciliation and the Geopolitics of Venture Capital
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Sovereign Dilemma: A Critical Analysis of Startup Re-Domiciliation and the Geopolitics of Venture Capital
detail.abstract: The paper is a critical analysis of the geopolitical and fiscal implications of the new requirement of mandatory corporate re-domiciliation, or flipping, by the world leaders in the venture capital (VC) industry, and specifically Y Combinator (YC), to startups with high potential and emerging market origins. The research synthesises two conflicting theoretical approaches, the VC Efficiency Model, which promotes risk reduction through legal predictability, and the Financial Neo-Colonialism Critique that assumes the structural imperative of extraction. The approach includes a comprehensive Critical Qualitative Review of legal requirements, economic literature, and regulatory responses, to which the empirical modelling of the different fiscal outcomes is added. The evidence confirms the flip, although being a vital channel of international institutional capital, does structurally support wealth transfer by requiring the centralisation of Intellectual Property (IP) and imposing systematic profit stripping by employing aggressive transfer pricing practices. This procedure undermines the domestic tax base in the long term and places founders under a difficult and cumbersome bi-compliance regime (FEMA/ODI). One of the most important things is that the detailed analysis, incorporating the empirical modelling and the case studies of fintech giants Razorpay and Groww, unveils the estimated financial gains to the parent jurisdiction and the measurable fiscal losses suffered by India. It is concluded that YC is a structural gatekeeper that creates systemic capital concentration that requires targeted and specific policy interventions to completely depreciate the historical benefit of foreign domicile.

reference: LSE Legal Studies Working Paper No. 24/2025
title: Feminist Jurisprudence, Personal Liberation, and Hope
affiliations: School of Law, Royal Holloway University of London

detail.title: Feminist Jurisprudence, Personal Liberation, and Hope

publicationDetails.detailsText: LSE Legal Studies Working Paper No. 24/2025
publicationDetails.journalName: LSE Law School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Global examples evidence the failure of achieving, and backlash against, gender equality, contributing to a need to revisit feminist jurisprudence and its methods. This paper examines aspects of feminist theories highlighting how law participates in removing hope for gender equality and justice, but also how feminists suggest ways to reimagine law differently with the hope of bringing positive change, aiming for gender justice. The paper focuses on women's liberation and social conditions of freedom before connecting personal liberation to hope oriented to action-an ordinary, horizontal hope in and through our everyday lives that law frames, scaffolds and socially structures. The author argues that, through these practices in which everyone can participate, there is hope of liberation, of freedom as creativity, developing the capacities of each unique person, an emancipatory project in a hope for epistemic justice.

title: Scoring for Good: The Performance of Performance-Based Pledge Donations
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Scoring for Good: The Performance of Performance-Based Pledge Donations
detail.abstract: In this paper we investigate a novel fundraising mechanism, Performance-Based Pledges (PBPs), where donors give a fixed amount each time a specific event occurs. We test the efficacy of PBPs in two pre-registered online experiments (n=1050) tied to real sporting events. We complement this with observational data from an independent PBP fundraising campaign. We find that PBPs serve as an effective complement to traditional one-off donations both in the proportion of donors and total funds raised. In addition, a substantial fraction of donors preferred PBPs to traditional one-off donations when given the choice, warranting their inclusion in fundraising campaigns. Finally, we find that PBPs can attract recurring donors and mitigate uncertainty in donations when implemented across multiple events. Taken together, these results provide actionable guidance for charities seeking to diversify their funding strategies.

title: On Dialogic Relations Transforming from Monologic to Dialogic
affiliations: Rutgers University

detail.title: On Dialogic Relations Transforming from Monologic to Dialogic
detail.abstract:
Although we live in an era of unprecedented global connectivity, authentic connectednesswhere new possibilities are co-created among people-remains elusive. Western individualist culture, grounded in a monologic and instrumental "I-It" relational structure, reinforces separation, hierarchy, and adversarial discourse.
This paper proposes a dialogic alternative to human relating that repositions the self and other within a relational, co-constructive framework rooted in mutual accountability, inclusivity, and shared equality based meaning-making. Drawing on two decades of practice in democratic and dialogic education in Israel and global practice as a conflict, dialogue, and mediation professional, the paper introduces a reflective–action model integrating insight (reflection on assumptions and perceptions of self, other, and relation) and action (participative practices that embed new understandings of relating in daily life). Illustrative cases—from democratic and dialogic school leadership transformation to business education—demonstrate the power of dialogic practices to rebuild trust, foster belonging, and sustain collaboration. Through this exploration, the paper argues that moving from an individualistic to a relational unit of analysis can help counter social fragmentation and cultivate more caring, mutually responsible, and dialogically engaged communities.

title: Great Expectations or False Hopes? The Case of Sustainable Finance
affiliations: London School of Economics - Law School

detail.title: Great Expectations or False Hopes? The Case of Sustainable Finance

publicationDetails.detailsText: LSE Legal Studies Working Paper No. 30/2025
publicationDetails.journalName: LSE Law School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper assesses whether sustainable finance can compensate for inadequate governmental action on climate change. While initiatives such as the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ) have raised expectations that financial markets can drive the net-zero transition, evidence suggests these hopes are overstated. The analysis demonstrates that the effectiveness of sustainable finance is fundamentally contingent on legal and regulatory frameworks, as well as broader political economy dynamics. Absent explicit or implicit legal endorsement, reliance on financial markets risks fostering misplaced optimism and delaying necessary governmental action to achieve the Paris Agreement targets.
