title: The Global Law of Debt
affiliations: Harvard Law School and University of Cambridge, Faculty of Law

detail.title: The Global Law of Debt

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Public Law Working Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Harvard Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Corporate debt financing and the restructuring of large corporations are now governed by what this Article calls the “global law of debt,” a transnational system shaped more by law firms, investment banks, and investors in New York and London than by national laws or court decisions. Large companies can now optimize governing law on a transaction-by-transaction basis, for example by borrowing in New York and then restructuring that debt in the United Kingdom, or by borrowing in London through English-law governed contracts with New York-law interpretation for select provisions.  This Article provides the first account of this development, tracing its origins to the 1960s, when New York and London debt professionals expanded into each other’s markets, creating an entangled system that fostered mutual learning and competition.  In 1978, Congress enacted a new bankruptcy law that gave American lawyers and investors corporate restructuring expertise that they later exported abroad.  In the post-pandemic era, London emerged as a global restructuring hub rivaling the United States.  These developments have produced a robust global debt market, but they have also unsettled long-standing assumptions about the rights of creditors as Chapter 11’s primacy fades and controversial American innovations that erode creditor protections proliferate globally.

reference: LSE Legal Studies Working Paper No. 34
title: Regulating the Digital Economy in the EU: The Hope of Redistribution
affiliations: Sciences Po

detail.title: Regulating the Digital Economy in the EU: The Hope of Redistribution

publicationDetails.detailsText: LSE Legal Studies Working Paper No. 34
publicationDetails.journalName: LSE Law School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper contends that the hope to redistribute technological and economic power from non-European to European companies permeates the current 'tech regulation' frenzy at the European Union (EU). While regulations like the Digital Markets Act and the AI Act are often criticised as stifling rather than supporting innovation, there is more than one reason to believe that the EU shouldn't lose hope just yet. In areas of strategic political importance like AI, it is sensible for the EU to regulate at the Union level rather than leaving the task to 27 Member States. Concerns about excessive compliance costs for small firms may also be overstated, since most obligations apply only to larger companies, and the EU has committed to providing regulatory support to start-ups. Economic formulae to boost innovation that work in other places may not be suited to the fabric of European societies. All things considered, the EU's tech regulations have the potential to help redistribute economic and technological power globally in favour of European companies. But a lot hinges on whether and how these regulations are enforced, and whether they are supported by broader EU innovation policies. Only time will tell whether hope will sustain effective enforcement and support for the European innovation ecosystem.

title: Why They Disagree: Decoding Differences in Opinions about AI Risk on the Lex Fridman Podcast
affiliations: Emory University, INSEAD and Sabanci University

detail.title: Why They Disagree: Decoding Differences in Opinions about AI Risk on the Lex Fridman Podcast

publicationDetails.journalName: INSEAD Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The emergence of transformative technologies often surfaces deep societal divisions, nowhere more evident than in contemporary debates about artificial intelligence (AI). A striking feature of these divisions is that they persist despite shared interests in ensuring that AI benefits humanity and avoiding catastrophic outcomes. This paper analyzes contemporary debates about AI risk, parsing the differences between the “doomer” and “boomer” perspectives into definitional, factual, causal, and moral premises to identify key points of contention. We find that differences in perspectives about existential risk (“X-risk”) arise fundamentally from differences in causal premises about design vs. emergence in complex systems, while differences in perspectives about employment risks (“E-risks”) pertain to different causal premises about the applicability of past theories (evolution) vs their inapplicability (revolution). Disagreements about these two forms of AI risk appear to share two properties: neither involves significant disagreements on moral values and both can be described in terms of differing views on the extent of boundedness of human rationality. Our approach to analyzing reasoning chains at scale, using an ensemble of LLMs to parse textual data, can be applied to identify key points of contention in debates about risk to the public in any arena.

title: Role of Innovative Processes to Improve the Safety, Security and Quality of Food: A Conceptual Study

detail.title: Role of Innovative Processes to Improve the Safety, Security and Quality of Food: A Conceptual Study
detail.abstract: Food safety and food security remain urgent global priorities as the world population surges and food systems face technological, environmental, and socioeconomic challenges. Advancements in novel food processing technologies such as pulsed electric field processing, high-pressure processing, and hurdle technology have contributed significantly to improving food safety and extending shelf life without compromising nutritional and sensory quality. The agriculture and food supply chain has evolved into a complex, multi-stakeholder system influenced by external forces including climate change, governance, industrialization, and globalization. Increasing consumer expectations for high-quality, safe, nutritious, and affordable food demand continuous innovation. This conceptual study examines the role of innovative technologies in enhancing food safety, quality, and security, highlighting modern industry practices, emerging solutions, challenges, and future prospects. It also emphasizes the need for integrated policy, scientific research, and stakeholder collaboration to ensure safe and sustainable food systems globally.

title: Mandating the Impossible? Assessing Canada’s Electric Vehicle Mandate for 2026 and Beyond
affiliations: University of Calgary

detail.title: Mandating the Impossible? Assessing Canada’s Electric Vehicle Mandate for 2026 and Beyond
detail.abstract:
• Until September 5, 2025, when it was waived by Prime Minister Carney, Canada’s federal Zero Emissions Vehicle (ZEV) mandate for 2026 required 20 percent of new light-vehicle sales to be ZEVs, equivalent to 380,000 units. This paper shows why the federal government had to waive the requirement. Based on projected sales of 1.9 million vehicles, actual 2026 ZEV sales are forecast at only 270,000, which would have created a shortfall of 110,000 units.

• The prime minister also announced that the federal government was conducting a 60-day review of the policy itself, which requires new light-vehicle sales to be 100 percent comprised of ZEVs by 2035. This paper shows why such a review was needed: the targets are similarly unattainable beyond 2026. As a result of not meeting the target, automakers, under the scheme, might have had to collectively spend a considerable sum of money in 2026 – an unknown amount to purchase Excess Credits and over $200 million to create Charging Fund Credits for investing in charging station infrastructure.

• Given these penalties, manufacturers in this scenario might have had to comply with the required percentage by restricting sales of non-ZEVs. Further, such regulatory constraints could have reduced vehicle supply by over 400,000 vehicles in 2026. Economic constraints driven by the potential cost of credits relative to the benefits of selling non-ZEVs could further reduce sales by as many as 50,000 vehicles. Such reductions in sales would leave significant consumer demand unmet.

• Firms such as Tesla, Kia, Hyundai, Mitsubishi, Volvo, BMW, and Rivian, which can exceed the 20 percent threshold, stand to gain windfall revenues from selling excess credits. Meanwhile, Canadian-based producers such as GM, Ford, Toyota, Stellantis, and Honda would face higher costs and reduced competitiveness.

• This paper recommends looking at a blend of policy options to address the problem, if the policy is not abandoned altogether. First and most obvious, revise the current trajectory for the mandated percentage of ZEV sales to align with consumer preferences and with the actual availability of vehicles, as discussed in Livingston (2024). Second, send the proceeds from the sale of Excess Credits to the federal government. Third, count pure or non-plug-in hybrids (and not just plug-in hybrids) towards mandated targets.1 Fourth, suspend the ZEV mandate until the shape of Canada’s auto industry – and availability of ZEVs on the market – are made clearer by the outcome of negotiations between Canada and the United States regarding new US tariffs and between Canada and China, the world’s largest exporter of electric cars.

detail.abstract: We examine why and when institutional investors disclose the rationales behind their proxy voting decisions, a transparency practice that has expanded rapidly over the past decade. Using novel data on over 33 million votes cast at U.S. firms by institutional investors worldwide, we show that the decision to disclose rationales is mainly an institution-level policy that is highly persistent, driven by stewardship incentives, client demands, and institutional norms. The implementation of this policy, however, is context-driven and triggered by uncertainty: using machine learning, we document that disclosure is more likely when voting against management or when deviating from expectations. This suggests that rationales convey information beyond investors’ general voting policies. Finally, consistent with some investors deriving benefits from disclosing voting rationales, we observe that institutions experience growth in assets under management after adopting this policy. Our study documents that voting rationales serve as a mechanism for enhancing transparency and accountability in corporate governance.

title: Joint Investment or Green Reshoring? Multinational Firm's Global Production and Social Impact Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: The growing emphasis on product sustainability is reshaping the global production strategies of multinational firms (MNFs), where notable asymmetries exist between developed and developing markets in terms of production costs and consumer green concerns. Consider an MNF that relies on an overseas manufacturer (OM) located in developing countries with a cost advantage for production and sells products to consumers with significant green concern in developed markets. Will the MNF make a complementary green investment with the overseas manufacturer, or decide on green reshoring to resolve the issue? In this study, we formulate the MNF's key tradeoffs between overseas production and local production (green reshoring). Cost-benefit analysis shows that: (1) Joint green investments by the MNF and the OM may generate either a virtuous or a vicious cycle of emission reduction, depending on the MNF's green investment efficiency. (2) Overseas production causes total GHG emissions to first rise and then fall as the market potential difference widens, suggesting that indiscriminate reshoring may, counterintuitively, increase overall emissions. (3) MNF can enhance consumer surplus either by encouraging the overseas manufacturer to jointly invest in GHG emission reductions or by utilizing the manufacturer's price leverage over it to reduce the overall procurement costs. This paper highlights the importance of regional differences and supply chain interactions in shaping the global production strategies of MNFs, prompting policymakers to balance firms' profits, consumer welfare, and the resulting environmental impact.

detail.abstract:
Project objective: To analyze the current state of the Kazakhstan stock market, identify key development challenges, and propose practical measures to improve liquidity, the range of instruments, and strengthen the investment culture. 
Subject of the study: The processes and mechanisms of the Kazakhstan stock market, including regulatory aspects, liquidity, and investor accessibility. 

Hypothesis: Low stock liquidity and the underdeveloped KASE stock market segment are due to a limited selection of instruments and a weak investment culture. The launch of market-making and the participation of pension funds, the creation of local ETFs, and educational initiatives for young people will lead to increased turnover and a broader investor base. 

Research procedure: The study analyzed KASE and NBK statistics (2015–2024), calculated indicators of capitalization, liquidity, and concentration, compared results with international markets, and included a school survey and an investor interview. 

Research methods: Statistical and regression analysis, index construction (Amihud, turnover), difference-in-differences method, sociological surveys, and expert interviews. Novelty: The study links quantitative analysis with practical solutions, combining market making, local ETFs, and an educational app in one framework. 

Results and conclusions: The market shows low stock share (2–3%), fewer issuers, and weak engagement. Proposed solutions can narrow spreads, raise turnover, and keep capital inside the country. 

Practical significance of the study: The measures can be applied by KASE and regulators to enhance liquidity, build a stable investor base, and support economic diversification.

title: Domain-oriented vs. Sales-oriented Communication: Which Holds the Key in Livestreaming Commerce?
affiliations: , University of Oxford, Saïd Business School and School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University

detail.title: Domain-oriented vs. Sales-oriented Communication: Which Holds the Key in Livestreaming Commerce?
detail.abstract: Effective communication is crucial for real-time, human-in-the-loop service systems, yet it’s often overlooked as a designable operational tool in operations management. This study explores how communication content design impacts performance in livestreaming commerce, where time and cognitive constraints are prominent. We distinguish between two content types: sales-oriented communication, which accelerates decision-making, and domain-oriented communication, which enhances decision reliability. Drawing on Information Processing and Dual-System Theory, we conceptualize livestreaming as an information–capacity system, where performance depends on aligning content with audiences' cognitive readiness. Analyzing 1,140 hours of jade livestreams using large language models, we find a speed-reliability trade-off: sales-oriented communication boosts product sales more than twice as much as domain-oriented communication, but it also increases product returns. Mechanism analyses reveal that emotional arousal, temporal sequencing, and contextual factors influence content effectiveness. Specifically, sales-oriented communication excels under high emotional arousal, especially negative emotions, and in low-stakes, heuristic-rich conditions. In contrast, domain-oriented communication thrives when cognitive capacity is abundant. A counterfactual simulation suggests that aligning content with cognitive readiness can increase sales by 25%, reduce returns by 53%, and boost net revenue by 132%. These findings highlight communication content design as a strategic lever for optimizing service performance.

detail.abstract: Firms that encounter lawsuits are subject to unforeseen costs when a case is ruled in favor of the plaintiff. We examine the impact of lawsuits brought against firms and whether this affects the firms' dividend policy, using unique hand-collected datasets of employee litigations and disputes that include court settlements for employee dispute cases in the United States. We find that lawsuits lower a firm's payout ratio, and an increase in lawsuits for a firm lowers the likelihood of the firm to pay out dividends. The payout ratio also declines for firms following a litigation year: this effect of a lower payout ratio is more pronounced for smaller firms. These findings provide evidence that firms adjust their dividend policy when facing employee lawsuits.

detail.abstract: We investigate what narratives can influence the Indonesian public to be more receptive to progressive policies and development ideas centered on social justice and the environment. We conduct an online experiment randomly exposing participants to a short narrative about the Indonesian economy. Each narrative appeals to different principles, from equal opportunity to environmental protection. We find that each narrative has its merits and flaws. The narrative that calls for preventing development from displacing people and damaging the environment, along with the narrative that emphasizes human development, shows the most promise in cultivating people's receptivity. Meanwhile, narratives that call for rebalancing economic distribution and promoting equal opportunity have a limited impact and even generate backlash against progressive ideas. We also find that simpler messages are more effective in shifting perceptions. Conjoint analysis affirms that environmental protection is not a paramount concern for the Indonesian public. Our insights will inform the policy advocacy work of many think tanks and may help civil society organizations wage more effective campaigns.

detail.abstract: Work-Family Conflict (WFC) has become a pressing concern in health systems worldwide, particularly for nurses whose professional and domestic roles often overlap. In Ghana, where traditional gender roles assign caregiving responsibilities to women, female nurses face unique challenges balancing work and family life. This study investigates the relationship between work-family conflict and job satisfaction among female nurses, particularly the moderating role of social support from supervisors, co-workers, and family members. Guided by the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, the study employs a quantitative, survey-based design involving 210 female nurses across three major hospitals in Ghana's Western Region. Using validated instruments, data were analyzed through descriptive and inferential statistics to test hypotheses regarding the associations among WFC, job satisfaction, and sources of social support. Results indicate that higher levels of work-family conflict significantly reduce job satisfaction, but social support moderates this relationship. Supervisor and co-worker support showed stronger buffering effects than family support, though all three forms of support contributed positively. The study underscores the need for organizational and policy interventions to enhance social support mechanisms and mitigate the negative effects of work-family conflict on nurses' professional satisfaction. The findings contribute to the literature by situating the work-family interface within an African cultural and healthcare context and provide practical recommendations for policymakers, hospital administrators, and practitioners.

title: The Digital Womb: Cognitive Liberty and the Fight for our Sovereign Future
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Digital Womb: Cognitive Liberty and the Fight for our Sovereign Future

declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: We are living through a global coup against human rights. This is the central problem; an ontological crisis has become an existential one. The very processes of decision-making that fuel our other crises are rooted in a corrupted idea of humanity. While we fret over data privacy and screen time, a deeper, ontological war is being waged over the fundamental question: what does it mean to be human? I argue that our escalating immersion into the digital realm is not merely a technological shift but something akin to a third birth—a transition that opens vast new possibilities while at the same time violently hijacking the essential human journey. We long for psychological sovereignty and wholeness; instead, we are fed division and meaninglessness. This hijacking threatens to dislodge the entire Enlightenment project, detaching it from any idea of a collective humanity. Author Terrence McKenna imagined the 'singularity' as a transcendental attractor at the end of time—a point toward which human evolution accelerates until transformation becomes so rapid that our old models of "the human" collapse. For him, this was a breakthrough in consciousness, language, and perception—not just machines outpacing us, but humanity outgrowing itself. My concern is that we are entering this accelerated phase precisely when multiple global crises demand a collective human response. (As opposed to an individual response like ‘meditating to become one with the universe’ or to ‘see the illusory nature of reality’). And the forces driving this singularity are the same ones actively preventing such collectivity. The extreme individualism born from post-WWII prosperity and the 1960s youth revolution has been hijacked, amplified to a point where we are rapidly losing the sense of ourselves as part of a larger, universal project.

title: The Maqasid Education Model: Restoring Purpose to Global Learning
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Maqasid Education Model: Restoring Purpose to Global Learning
detail.abstract: This paper confronts the global crisis of credentialism and skill mismatch-termed here as the "Educational Trap"-by proposing a restructured national education model grounded in maqasid al-shariah (the higher objectives of Islamic ethics). Conventional systems create a systemic bottleneck by prioritizing university degrees over practical competence, leading to graduate unemployment, massive student debt (Piketty & Goldhammer, 2022), and social inequality. Our model dismantles this paradigm by establishing a four-year professional senior high school (SMA) as the primary engine of the national workforce, while transforming universities into elite, state-funded research hubs. Through mandatory State-Industry Partnerships, the system guarantees a direct, dignified pathway from education to employment. This reform is designed not merely to serve the market, but to cultivate a workforce that is economically resilient, socially equitable, and ethically principled. This paper contributes to global policy discourse by offering a replicable model for countries seeking to realign moral values, fiscal efficiency, and labor productivity within education systems.

title: Government Subsidy V.S. Cooperative Advertising: Policy Design for SME Marketing under Rural Revitalization
affiliations: Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management, School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University, University of Oxford, Saïd Business School and University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee - Sheldon B. Lubar School of Business

detail.title: Government Subsidy V.S. Cooperative Advertising: Policy Design for SME Marketing under Rural Revitalization
detail.abstract: Supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) has become a central policy priority in efforts to revitalize rural economies. In many regions, local governments support SMEs in marketing their agricultural specialty products, which often face limited reach beyond local markets. This support primarily takes two forms: financial subsidies that partially reimburse marketing expenditures, and cooperative advertising, in which governments directly participate in promotional campaigns. This paper compares these alternative policy instruments and examines how they shape government-business interactions. We develop a Stackelberg game between a local government and a representative SME. The firm privately observes market conditions and decides whether to disclose this information before the government selects a policy instrument and support level. We further extend the analysis to a multi-firm setting to capture competition and marketing spillovers. Our results show that subsidies and cooperative advertising influence firm behavior through distinct channels and lead to different patterns of government intervention. Cooperative advertising is relatively more attractive to the government when the risk of market stagnation is high, whereas subsidies are favored in stronger markets. Anticipating such state-contingent policies, firm is more inclined to disclose demand information when market potential is sufficiently low or high. In multi-firm environments, the relative advantage of cooperative advertising is further amplified, particularly when products are highly substitutable.

title: Liabilities of Company Directors under Extant Nigerian Corporate Law: A Comprehensive Analysis
affiliations: Igbinedion University, Okada

detail.title: Liabilities of Company Directors under Extant Nigerian Corporate Law: A Comprehensive Analysis
detail.abstract: This article presents a comprehensive, critical analysis of the liabilities of company directors under extant Nigerian corporate law. Through meticulous examination of statutory provisions, judicial interpretations, and scholarly discourse, this article demonstrates that while the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020 represents significant legislative progress in codifying director duties and liabilities, its effectiveness is substantially undermined by judicial inconsistency in applying veil-piercing doctrines, the absence of a balanced protective framework for directors, and inadequate enforcement mechanisms. The article employs a multi-dimensional approach, incorporating doctrinal analysis, comparative perspectives from the United Kingdom and United States, and examination of emerging issues such as Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) liabilities. Through detailed examination of civil, criminal, and administrative liabilities, defences, mitigation strategies, and reform proposals, this article contributes to the scholarly discourse on corporate governance in Nigeria and provides practical insights for directors, legal practitioners, policymakers, and corporate governance stakeholders.

title: How Does Patient Capital Empower Supply Chains? An Empirical Investigation of Spillover Effects from Government-Guided Funds
affiliations: Capital University of Economics and Business and Capital University of Economics and Business

detail.title: How Does Patient Capital Empower Supply Chains? An Empirical Investigation of Spillover Effects from Government-Guided Funds
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of patient capital investment on alleviating the financing constraints of upstream and downstream firms in the supply chain. The findings reveal that patient capital investment generates a positive spillover effect within the supply chain, alleviating the financing constraints of core suppliers and customers. This spillover effect is more pronounced when the interdependency between supply chain firms is stronger and when the financing capacity of these key partners is weaker. Mechanism analysis indicates that patient capital operates through two channels: capital cost effect (improving accounts receivable turnover efficiency of suppliers) and credit expansion effect (increasing the proportion of credit loans for customers). Further analysis shows that this supply chain spillover effect significantly enhances the investment efficiency and innovation level of major suppliers and customers. The findings provide theoretical and empirical insights for policies aimed at fostering patient capital, promoting industrial and supply chain optimization and upgrading, and building a modern industrial system.

title: Economic Implications of AI-Driven Cybersecurity in Emerging Markets
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: Economic Implications of AI-Driven Cybersecurity in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: This study examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into cybersecurity frameworks within emerging markets, highlighting the economic implications and technological challenges involved. It explores how AI-driven security measures can enhance threat detection, reduce cybercrime losses, and improve operational efficiency, thereby contributing to economic resilience and growth. The analysis addresses infrastructural constraints, workforce skill gaps, and governance factors that influence adoption, emphasizing the importance of tailored strategies for diverse economic and cultural contexts. The role of AI techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and federated learning is discussed in relation to their application in real-time threat intelligence, automated incident response, and anomaly detection. The paper also considers policy frameworks, regulatory compliance, and international cooperation as critical enablers for sustainable cybersecurity ecosystems. Furthermore, it investigates the potential for indigenous AI solutions, regional collaboration, and innovation hubs to stimulate local capacity and economic diversification. The findings underscore the necessity of comprehensive approaches combining technological innovation, workforce development, and governance reforms to build resilient digital infrastructures that support secure trade, attract investment, and promote inclusive growth in emerging economies.

title: The Colonial Legacy of Power, Profit, and Prejudice in Global Health Governance
affiliations: University of Nairobi and University of Nairobi - School of Law

detail.title: The Colonial Legacy of Power, Profit, and Prejudice in Global Health Governance
detail.abstract: Th is article examines how colonial legacies continue to structure global health fi nancing and governance, perpetuating systemic inequities between the Global North and South, particularly African countries. Historical analysis reveals that colonial health systems were strategically designed to protect European interests while exploiting indigenous populations and establishing racially segregated frameworks whose structural biases persist in contemporary institutions. International fi nancial architecture, particularly through bodies such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, reinforces these asymmetries through governance mechanisms that privilege wealthy nations in decision-making and resource allocation. Th e COVID-19 pandemic exposed these entrenched disparities, as vaccine nationalism and disparate fi scal capacities widened the existing health gaps. Emerging digital health technologies now risk establishing new extractive relationships, as health data harvested from vulnerable populations fl ows to high-income countries without adequate benefi t-sharing frameworks, a pattern identifi ed as data colonialism. Addressing these interconnected challenges requires decolonising global health governance through fundamental reforms that redistribute power, ensure data sovereignty, and centre historically marginalised voices in shaping health priorities and fi nancing mechanisms.

title: The Authority of the UN General Assembly to Implement the Responsibility to Protect Through the Establishment of an International Protection Force: Revisiting the “Uniting for Peace” Resolution
affiliations: High Court of Kenya

detail.title: The Authority of the UN General Assembly to Implement the Responsibility to Protect Through the Establishment of an International Protection Force: Revisiting the “Uniting for Peace” Resolution

keywords.keywords: Responsibility to Protect (R2P) and UN General Assembly Authority

contentFormat.other: It is a policy brief addressed to the global governance institutions

detail.abstract: The recurring paralysis of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) due to veto power politics has severely undermined global efforts to prevent mass atrocities, intervene in humanitarian catastrophes, and uphold the Responsibility to Protect (R2P). The Uniting for Peace Resolution (UNGA Resolution 377A (V) of 1950) provides a critical, although contested, legal avenue for the UN General Assembly (UNGA) to assume a more assertive role when the Security Council fails to act due to lack of unanimity among its permanent members. This policy brief evaluates whether the UN General Assembly possesses the authority to implement R2P by establishing an International Protection Force (IPF) in conflict-torn regions where the Security Council is disabled by vetoes, geopolitical stalemates, or deadlocks. It builds on legal analysis of UN Charter provisions, the practice of the UNGA, precedent cases, advisory opinions, and the jurisprudential trajectory of R2P since its adoption in the 2005 World Summit Outcome Document. This brief concludes that yes, the UN General Assembly has credible legal, normative, and precedential grounds to authorize an IPF under the Uniting for Peace mechanism provided that the force is framed as a collective measure for maintaining international peace and security, not punitive enforcement action in violation of Article 2(7) of the UN Charter. Past UNGA actions, including in the Korean War (1950), Suez Crisis (1956), Afghanistan (1980), Syria (2016), and Ukraine (2022-2023), demonstrate the Assembly's capacity to mobilize peace-preserving operations, impose collective measures, and even recommend the use of armed force.

detail.abstract:
Commercial cleaning is a high-risk, high-variability industry that has been relatively understudied in the operations management literature despite having material implications for occupational safety, indoor environmental quality, organizational liability, and public health. Peer-reviewed research indicates high rates of musculoskeletal disorders, slips, trips and falls (STFs), and chemical exposures among janitorial workers, alongside systemic underreporting of injuries (Anderson et al., 2022; Bitzas et al., 2022; Charles et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2022).Yet the industry lacks a standardized, data-driven framework to reduce variance, validate hygiene performance, and systematically improve outcomes.

This working paper presents the SGHG Six Sigma Method™, a proprietary Lean Six Sigma framework designed specifically for commercial cleaning, organized around four integrated pillars: Safety, Green, Hygiene, and Growth. The framework was developed using a mixed-methods, multiple-embedded case study design (Yin, 2018), supported by a six-month Measurement System Analysis (MSA) study and validated through operational implementation at SGHG Cleaning LLC facilities. The method is based on the use of sector-specific key performance indicators (KPIs) (Slip Hazard Index [SHI], Chemical Efficiency Ratio [CER], ATP Hygiene Variance Score and Ergonomic Load Score [ELS]) that are evidence-based and derived from safety science, ergonomics, indoor environmental health and hygiene verification research (Allen & MacNaughton, 2017; Dancer, 2014; Harding-Smith et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2023; Powell et al., 2013).

The SGHG Six Sigma Method™ was implemented in eight commercial buildings. The result was statistically significant improvements in slip-hazard conditions, ergonomic loads, hygiene variance and chemical efficiency as well as Cp, Cpk. The framework advances Lean Six Sigma into a previously under-theorized service domain, offering a replicable model for commercial cleaning providers, facility managers, and researchers.

title: Human-Centered AI for Real-Time Self-Checkout Assistance: An Event-Driven Architecture with Human-in-the-Loop Decision Support for Enhanced Customer Experience and Shrink Reduction

detail.title: Human-Centered AI for Real-Time Self-Checkout Assistance: An Event-Driven Architecture with Human-in-the-Loop Decision Support for Enhanced Customer Experience and Shrink Reduction
detail.abstract: Self-checkout systems provide convenience and operational scalability for retailers but introduce recurring issues such as delayed assistance, inconsistent triage during peak traffic, and high false-positive alerts from automated security mechanisms. This paper proposes a human-centered, event-driven AI architecture that treats AI as decision support rather than autonomous enforcement. The system prioritizes assistance events using a multi-factor scoring model based on wait time, anomaly likelihood, contextual complexity, and associate workload, while preserving human discretion as the final decision-maker. The approach is evaluated using a simulation study calibrated to realistic retail traffic and checkout event patterns. A synthetic dataset of over 800,000 transactions across twelve representative store profiles is used to compare baseline manual triage with the proposed human-centered AI workflow. The results indicate a substantial reduction in average assistance wait time and a decrease in false alerts, while maintaining high coverage of genuinely risky events. The findings highlight managerial implications for retailers by showing how AI-assisted prioritization can reduce cognitive load, support fairer and more consistent interventions, and improve associate productivity without compromising autonomy or trust.

title: LLM-Augmented Social Simulation in Applied Ethics: Addressing the Ideal World Objection
affiliations: University of Milan

detail.title: LLM-Augmented Social Simulation in Applied Ethics: Addressing the Ideal World Objection
detail.abstract: This paper suggests using Agent-Based Models augmented by Large Language Models in applied ethics research devoted to organisational and sector-wide governance. Through parallels with other forms of AI-assisted moral inquiry, it argues that these tools can support research grounded in rule consequentialism and principle contractualism by facilitating exploratory approaches that guide further empirical analysis. These exploratory studies can contribute to assessing and formulating rules and principles that resist the Ideal World Objection (IWO), as well as to developing strategies for implementing them at optimal compliance rates. To this end, these simulations must allow researchers to observe and act upon variables such as the expected compliance rate of a rule or principle and the expected value associated with different compliance rates. Additional variables may be relevant depending on the specific study undertaken, the normative theory on which it relies, and the possible solution to the IWO that the research might endorse or wish to test.

title: Algorithmic Infrastructures of Attention: A Formal Model of AI, Lock-In, and Governance

detail.title: Algorithmic Infrastructures of Attention: A Formal Model of AI, Lock-In, and Governance
detail.abstract: How do shared AI and data infrastructure reshape strategic attention and create the risk of system-level lock-in? Building on the attention-based view (ABV), we develop a formal model in which organizational decision makers allocate scarce attention across options based on hybrid human-AI signals. AI intensity reduces signal noise, but when models and data are widely shared, it increases cross-firm signal correlation, yielding a precision-correlation trade-off. Attention follows a softmax rule; therefore, more precise and more correlated signals, combined with capacity bottlenecks, generate an inverted-U relationship between AI intensity and performance, and a region we term algorithmic lock-in, where attention is narrowly concentrated and sluggish to adjust. We show how data proprietariness, internal democratization of attention, human-AI weighting, focus intensity, and minimum exploration floors shift the shape and location of this inverted-U and shrink or expand the basin of the algorithmic lock-in. The model formalizes "algorithmic infrastructures of attention" as a core structural element of ABV in the AI era and links them to governance choices over the design of human-AI collaboration in strategic decision processes.

title: The economic consequences of introducing rescissionary private rights of action in the investment fund industry

detail.title: The economic consequences of introducing rescissionary private rights of action in the investment fund industry

keywords: Oxford University Bank v. Lansuppe Feeder
FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

publicationDetails.detailsText: UCLA School of Law, Public Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of California, Los Angeles School of Law, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In Oxford University Bank v. Lansuppe Feeder, LLC, 933 F.3d 99 (2d Cir. 2019) ("OUB"), the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit held that §47(b) of the Investment Company Act ("ICA") implies a broad private right of action that enables the parties to a contract that violates the act to seek rescission of the contract. After OUB, commentators predicted that the decision would result in a significant increase in shareholder activism against closed-end funds (CEFs) and a sharp decline in the number of funds available in the market. This paper examines those predictions. The results show that OUB does not appear to be responsible for significant changes in activism or a reduction in the number of CEFs. In the baseline estimations, in which I consider a short sample period around OUB (one year before and after), I do not find significant changes in activism or the incidence of CEFs. If I consider a longer period (five years before and after OUB), I find an increase in activism, but that result seems more plausibly attributable to other factors-and especially changes in the law of control share acquisition provisions. I also find a decline in the number of CEFs relative to other public companies in this longer sample period; however, CEFs were already declining in absolute terms before OUB, and although the decline in CEFs relative to other public companies became more pronounced after the decision, that result is explained by a sharp increase in the number of other public companies, not a decline in the number of CEFs. These results have implications for FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund, Ltd., in which the Supreme Court will resolve the circuit split created by the Second Circuit. In particular, the results suggest that although rescissionary rights provide leverage to shareholder activists, that leverage does not appear to be a first-order determinant of activism or a sponsor's decision to operate a CEF.

title: Trials Avoid High Risk Patients and Underestimate Drug Harms
affiliations: Yale School of Management, Harvard University and Massachusetts General Hospital

detail.title: Trials Avoid High Risk Patients and Underestimate Drug Harms

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The FDA does not formally regulate representativeness, but if trials under-enroll vulnerable patients, the resulting evidence may understate harm from drugs. We study the relationship between trial participation and the risk of drug-induced adverse events for cancer medications using data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program linked to Medicare claims. Initiating treatment with a cancer drug increases the risk of hospitalization due to serious adverse events (SAE) by 2 percentage points per month (a 250% increase). Heterogeneity in SAE treatment effects can be predicted by patient's comorbidities, frailty, and demographic characteristics. Patients at the 90th percentile of the risk distribution experience a 2.5 times greater increase in SAEs after treatment initiation compared to patients at the 10th percentile of the risk distribution yet are 4 times less likely to enroll in trials. The predicted SAE treatment effects for the drug's target population are 15% larger than the predicted SAE treatment effects for trial enrollees, corresponding to 1 additional induced SAE hospitalization for every 25 patients per year of treatment. We formalize conditions under which regulating representativeness of SAE risk will lead to more externally valid trials, and we discuss how our results could inform regulatory requirements.

title: Patient Peer Effects: Evidence from Nursing Home Room Assignments
affiliations: and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: Patient Peer Effects: Evidence from Nursing Home Room Assignments

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We provide causal evidence that patient peer effects generate mortality impacts comparable to provider quality differences. Drawing on administrative records covering 2.6 million stays (2000–2010) across 7,200 U.S. nursing homes, we exploit plausibly exogenous roommate assignments identified through unique room identifiers. We estimate that assignment to a roommate diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) or Alzheimer’s disease related dementias (ADRD), relative to placement in a private room, increases 90-day mortality by 2.1 percentage points (14% of baseline)—equivalent to receiving care at a nursing home one full standard deviation worse in quality. Effects differ sharply by patient type: patients with AD/ADRD benefit substantially from cognitively healthy roommates but not from private rooms, suggesting important peer monitoring and support roles. In contrast, mortality of patients without AD/ADRD does not depend on roommate cognitive health but is reduced in private rooms. A simple assignment rule exploiting this heterogeneity could reduce overall mortality by 0.8 percentage points without additional resources.

title: Medicaid Coverage and Postpartum Opioid Use Disorder Treatment
affiliations: Indiana University, Indianapolis, Johns Hopkins University, George Mason University and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Medicaid Coverage and Postpartum Opioid Use Disorder Treatment

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Opioid use disorder (OUD) among pregnant women in the United States has risen more than fourfold since 1999, making substance use a leading cause of maternal mortality. Medicaid finances the majority of births and substance use disorder treatment in the U.S., yet until recently, coverage typically ends 60 days postpartum, potentially disrupting care continuity. The American Rescue Plan of 2021 extends postpartum Medicaid coverage from two months to 12 months, creating a natural experiment to evaluate the impact of coverage on access to medications for OUD (MOUD), the gold-standard treatment. We use linked nationwide all-payer medical and retail pharmacy claims from IQVIA in a difference-in-differences framework comparing postpartum MOUD continuity between Medicaid- and commercially-insured parents with a prenatal history of MOUD use. Extended Medicaid postpartum coverage increases Medicaid-financed MOUD months by 8.55%, the likelihood of continuing MOUD beyond 60 days by 5.12%, and total MOUD supply days by 7.99%. These gains are slightly offset by other payer reductions, yet result in a net 5.10% increase in overall MOUD months and 4.64% rise in treatment adherence. Findings highlight the importance of coverage duration as a practical lever to sustain MOUD treatment in the crucial first year after delivery period.
